articles.title: When Workers, Driving Customers or Saving Lives in the ER, Become Independent Contractors
articles.author: Boston DSA
articles.content: [[{“value”:” By: Matt Wolfinger BOSTON – There’s a loophole in our labor laws spreading across the economy. From delivery drivers to nurses, corporations are classifying workers as independent contractors and using the promise of flexible work to cudgel labor rights. Nearly 12 million people in the United States, or seven percent of the workforce, describe independent contractor work as their primary source of income, according to the most recent data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Independent contractors aren’t protected under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), so they can’t unionize, aren’t entitled to benefits, a minimum wage, or overtime and can be fired at will. Companies like Uber, Lyft and Amazon have spent hundreds of millions to keep their workers classified as self-employed independent contractors, allowing them to cut costs and indirectly union-bust. By blurring the line between employee and contractor, employers save money they’d otherwise be required to spend on unemployment insurance, benefits and employer-paid payroll taxes. Meanwhile, workers lcassified as contractors then pay exorbitantly higher taxation to account for both employee and employer contributions. If corporations can successfully “gigify” their industries, they can circumvent responsibilities and laws that would otherwise prevent them from mistreating their workers. 1099 tax filing, the paperwork for independent contractors (Working Mass) Uber, Lyft and the Legacy of Gigification Delivery and rideshare apps like Doordash, Lyft and Uber are poster children for operating in this gray area. Emerging in the shadow of the Great Recession when jobs were hard to come by, companies like Uber, Lyft and the now-defunct Sidecar pioneered the modern understanding of gig work by taking advantage of the dire economic landscape. In Massachusetts, most workers are considered employees unless a company can prove their work meets three different criteria. According to Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell’s office, the work must be: Done without the direction and control of the employer Performed outside the usual course of the employer’s business Done by someone who has their own, independent business or trade doing that kind of work Companies constantly find workarounds. In one landmark case, Massachusetts residents voted in late 2024 to pass a ballot measure affording rideshare drivers the right to unionize. Notably, neither Uber or Lyft spent a cent to oppose it. In contrast, they paid more than $200 million in California to help pass Proposition 22, a bill cementing California gig workers’ misclassification as independent contractors. The reason why these companies did not perceive Question 3 as a threat became clear in May, when over 70,000 Lyft and Uber in Massachusetts drivers successfully voted to certify their App Drivers Union (ADU). As the first union of its kind in the country, it’s a big deal—but there’s a catch: The union ceded on classification. Their official stance is that they’ve chosen to remain independent contractors. This limits the union’s ability to advocate for its members, since benefits like healthcare or a minimum wage are off the bargaining table. As Working Mass’s Editorial Board reported at the time, Question 3 “allowed drivers to vote for a collective bargaining representative, with which Uber and Lyft would then have to negotiate over wages and working conditions… [but only covers] app workers transporting passengers, leaving out take-out and grocery delivery workers.” As a result, “the system as written allows drivers to vote for or against collective bargaining but does not mandate any driver rights within the “union” once it is recognized.” This has led to credible accusations against the ADU of company unionism. The ADU’s FAQ page on their website states that remaining independent contractors allows members to “keep our flexibility and independence,” since bosses cannot legally dictate when independent contractors work and do not work. The ADU did not respond to requests for comment on how they reached this decision. App Drivers Union (ADU) marching in Labor Day 2026 (Working Mass) The flexibility messaging is reminiscent of a June 2026 report from the Flex Association, a national association for app-based work, that found that nearly two-thirds (63 percent) of the 10,000+ app-based workers they surveyed are doing gig work to supplement W-2 jobs. Flex’s 2024 Economic Impact Report found that “exactly half of driver and delivery partners would rather be able to choose their own hours, than receive a 50% increase in earnings with a fixed schedule.” While these studies seem to indicate gig workers would largely rather stay as independent contractors and prefer lower pay, there’s two fundamental flaws underpinning their results. First, drivers could advocate for having flexibility to choose their own hours and an increase in pay. There could also be an industry association for app-based work whose members include Uber, Lyft, Instacart, Doordash and Grubhub, Flex is incentivized to only share positive viewpoints on gig work. In reality, drivers aren’t a monolith—some have become disillusioned with the promises made to them by rideshare companies once the curtain is pulled back and their exploitation becomes indisputable. In July, a Massachusetts Uber driver filed a class action lawsuit against the company, alleging misclassification of its drivers as independent contractors. Uber uses this misclassification to avoid covering expenses like gas, insurance, and vehicle maintenance, since they were the responsibility of their “self-employed” contractor. It’s argued that the three qualifications in Massachusetts for independent contractor status aren’t met because: Uber controls the routes and pay of their drivers while requiring them to meet a set of standards dictated by the company, so the work is not done “without direction or control of the employer.” The services provided are not “performed outside the usual course of the employer’s business” (Uber is a company providing transportation to riders, which is fulfilled through the labor of their drivers). Drivers do not have “their own, independent business or trade doing that kind of work” as Uber sets pay rates, can change them at their sole discretion and requires a set of standards its drivers and vehicles must meet (and can change those at will). Food delivery and rideshare companies want to straddle the fence on employment, controlling every aspect of how drivers work through algorithms like employees, while stifling their ability to fully advocate for the same rights and benefits afforded to employees in Massachusetts. In 2024, More Perfect Union and Rideshare Guy put seven rideshare drivers in a room to see what fares they would be offered for identical trips and found that both Uber and Lyft’s algorithms routinely offered different prices to each driver. Uber’s average wage gap difference was roughly 12 cents. “You know, to the naked eye, it may not be as much,” driver and Senior Contributor to Rideshare Guy Sergio Avedian told More Perfect Union. However, “A penny’s difference on 2.7 billion trips that Uber does every quarter is the idea.” Nurses on strike during the lockout of July 2026 (Working Mass) The Gig Economy Taking Healthcare Executives in other industries have observed the chokehold platforms like Uber and Lyft have on their workers once they cannot do their job without it. Taking those lessons to heart, industries like healthcare have spent millions building their own. When nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH) with Brigham Nurses United (BNU) went on a one-day strike in July, the hospital locked them out for 4 additional days as retaliation, hiring 1,300 scab nurses to fill in for the 4,700 nurses on strike. Many of the scabs came from out-of-state, sourced from Colorado-based US Nursing (USN) who specialize in hiring nurses to scab during ongoing strikes. Similar to Amazon, they’ve begun outsourcing the labor to third-parties. Their website hosts a portal where nurses can apply to fill shifts at hospitals where “Potential Strikes” loom. The nurses taking over these positions are paid comparable wages than the nurses they’re replacing, but their lack of hands-on knowledge that comes from working full time at a hospital can place patients at an increased risk of harm. The job listings on “gig nursing” apps like Ingenovis Health’s often don’t list the facility in question, but anyone can make an account—no proof of credentials needed. Select “Strike Jobs” and set the location to Boston, MA to find nearly 300 USN listings, many of them starting October 11, for 2-week strike coverage at a hospital with a bed count of 846 and 59,715 emergency room visits. Two screenshots from the Ingenovis Health app listing an ICU RN position (start date October 11) and the facility details, captured October 8 (Working Mass). According to the American Hospital Directory, BWH has a bed count of 846, and their ED’s About page says they “care for nearly 60,000 patients each year.” The listing has since changed from an “Active Strike” to “Potential Strike” with a date of “TBA” after the MNA announced the strike’s postponement. 93 percent of the 4,000 workers with BNU recently voted in favor of an open-ended, indefinite strike, originally slated to start October 14. The decision came after their historic strike in July had yet to yield results at the bargaining table, with negotiations between the MNA and MGB leadership at a standstill. The strike has since been postponed pending a vote on what MGB calls its “last, best and final offer,” though the MNA has emphasized that MGB refuses to budge on many key issues or engage in more bargaining sessions. “Nurses continue seeking improvements on several key issues,” said an MNA spokesperson in a statement , including: … Limits on MGB’s reliance on temporary nurses to support continuity and quality of care; affordable health insurance with meaningful plan choice; a differential for nurses required to float among units; and a meaningful cost-of-living wage increase. Another strike is still on table if a contract fails to be ratified, even as MGB planned to once again work with USN to hire scabs for the strike. Since USN pays for each scab’s hotel and travel costs, they’re not classified as independent contractors. However, other gig nursing apps like CareRev have come under fire for allegedly misclassifying users as independent contractors. These platforms allegedly use a form of dynamic pricing to pay each nurse that looks at a listing an algorithmically generated pay rate, a difference of cents or even dollars apart. It’s unclear how these gig nursing algorithms function, but it’s eerily similar to the ones used by Uber and Lyft. The “gigification” of healthcare has earned gig nursing platforms the name “Uber for Nurses.” Central to the argument for gig nursing is in response to a so-called “nursing shortage.” But as recent data analysis from Time Magazine revealed , “there are substantively more actively licensed nurses than there are nursing jobs.” Framing the issue as a shortage obscures the real culprit—nurses are refusing to tolerate worsening working conditions. Dr. Katie Wells, a Senior Fellow at the AI Now Institute researching tech in healthcare, spoke to Working Mass : When I dug into the history of that, and I looked at all the scholars who had been studying labor markets for nurses, it became very clear that the rise of corporate medicine and the for-profit nature of a lot of hospital systems coincided with the degradation of working conditions for healthcare workers. Dr. Wells is the co-author of a two-part “Uber for Nursing” study detailing the rise of gig work in the healthcare industry. Although these platforms can be used to supply facilities with scabs, many are hired to account for lower levels of staffing. These platforms pit nurses against each other in a race to the bottom, where the nurse that wins a shift is the one willing to accept the lowest pay rate. Data the platform collects on nurses, such as credit card debt, helps it identify which nurses are more likely to accept lower pay. A portion of the travel nurses using these apps are classified as independent contractors. They don’t receive health benefits, despite providing others with healthcare themselves. These gig nursing platforms have been pushing for legislation that would classify the nurses who use their platforms as independent contractors. They’d be defined as different entities than existing healthcare staffing agencies, as AI Now’s study explains: “These platforms are trying to convince policymakers that their business model is not that of a healthcare staffing agency, and that they instead should be recognized as a ‘healthcare worker platform’ or a ‘healthcare technology platform.’” The language is similar to arguments made by Uber to Massachusetts legislators in 2024—that they’re closer to a “travel agency” than a transportation company—giving them the right to keep their drivers misclassified (a European court saw through this argument). That defense was part of a case brought against Uber and Lyft by then-Attorney General Maura Healey, who alleged they were misclassifying their drivers. The Classification Fight for Worker’s Rights In exchange for a $175 million settlement with Uber and Lyft, current AG Andrea Joy Campbell dropped the case before the court could rule whether rideshare drivers count as independent contractors. Campbell’s deal forced Uber and Lyft to abandon a similar ballot initiative to Prop. 22 in Massachusetts and afford drivers a few benefits. One of those benefits, which seemingly required the companies to pay drivers $32.50/hour, falls apart after reading the fine print . That pay rate only applies to “active hours,” meaning it counts the time when drivers are either on their way to pick up a rider or taking them to their destination, but not the time in-between, referred to as “online working hours.” “Time spent between trips, waiting for another ride request, or deadheading back from low-demand drop-off areas is neither compensated, nor counts towards the work time thresholds to qualify for sick time, health insurance stipends, and other benefits,” reporting from Forbes explains. Drivers have attested online that “staying busy the entire hour is impossible due to the oversaturation of drivers.” By comparing active time to online working hours, Forbes calculated the utilization rate (the percentage of time drivers actually get paid for): For example, if Uber pays $8 for a 12-minute trip, the driver’s pay rate per active hour would be $40 – above the mandated minimum. But if this is the only offer a driver receives and accepts over the next 48 minutes, the driver’s utilization rate would be 12/60= 20% (low!) and the gross pay per working hour would only be $8 (awful!). So, utilization rate is a critical determinant of driver earnings. This doesn’t include the burden on drivers of paying for gas and insurance, taking another chunk out of their pay. With employee status, drivers could bargain for a contract to cement a firm minimum wage. To their credit, Campbell’s office has kept their finger on the pulse of independent contractor misclassification. The AGO’s 2026 Labor day report released by its Fair Labor Division shows that in the last year, 1,500 workers across 60 companies were misclassified, leading to more than $2.1 million in penalties and restitution. “When workers are misclassified as independent contractors instead of employees, they are denied basic workplace rights, including guaranteed minimum wage, overtime pay, timely compensation, accrued sick leave, and more,” Campbell’s office stated in an emailed statement to Working Mass. “Addressing this harmful practice and ensuring that every worker receives the protections they deserve is one of my top priorities.” But until a firm decision is reached on how to classify rideshare and delivery drivers, a comprehensive answer on gig workers’ rights and the next steps organized labor will need to take will remain in limbo. There aren’t signs that federal reclassification is on the docket anytime soon, making the state level (for now) the best way forward. Although Campbell’s settlement took a similar bill to Prop. 22 off the ballot, gig work platforms have proven they’ll spend millions to tip the scales in their favor. Gig nursing platforms aren’t introducing legislation in Massachusetts that would reclassify their business like they have in other states, but that could always change. The conversation surrounding independent contracting finds itself in a sticky spot: many gig-workers prefer the flexibility provided by the work, and use it to supplement their income when their W-2 pay doesn’t cut it. Flexibility is attractive to workers, Dr. Wells explained, due to a lack of stable, guaranteed hours and a set schedule across the labor market. Knowing their schedules ahead of time gives workers more autonomy—scheduling a doctor’s visit or picking a child up from school becomes much easier. “I think the reality is that there is a problem with existing labor markets in so many of these sectors and, at large, that has real purchase,” said Dr. Wells. “It has so many things at play that it means people are willing to trade all kinds of protections for the allure or the possibility of flexible schedules.” The national minimum wage has sat at $7.25 since 2009, and the lack of universal healthcare is smothering everyday Americans in medical debt. The leading reported cause of bankruptcy in the U.S. is medical debt , and we’re the only major country without a form of universal healthcare. A long-term pathway to ending the exploitative nature of gig work and doing away with the independent contractor classification needs to come alongside ensuring workers don’t need to take on extra work to afford basic necessities, and without the threat of medical or student debt held over their heads. In a world where everyone is guaranteed a living wage and health benefits aren’t up to the whims of your employer, gig workers could stick with their 9 to 5 or even keep driving if that’s what they’d prefer. It may sound like a pipe dream, but the system as it stands puts the working class at a severe disadvantage. Drivers can choose to pick their main job that now pays them a living wage or stay a driver, earning a living wage and receiving the same health benefits that their other job afforded them. As companies celebrate record profits, the workers who generate that value see none of it reflected in their own paychecks. It’s undeniable that working as an independent contractor provides unmatched levels of autonomy, but that should not come at the cost of the benefits and workplace protections afforded as the bare minimum to every other worker in the country. “The rise of [gig nursing] is a symptom of really broken labor conditions,” Dr. Wells said. That’s how I try to think about it. And so when people say, ‘Well, let’s fix gig nursing,’ I think, ‘No, let’s fix the conditions that gave rise to gig nursing.’ Matt Wolfinger is a data journalist and a contributing writer to Working Mass. The post When Workers, Driving Customers or Saving Lives in the ER, Become Independent Contractors appeared first on Working Mass . “}]]

articles.title: Why I Started Judging the Judges: The Election That Changed How I Vote
articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. When I watched a tough-on-crime prosecutor reinvent himself before a room full of progressive voters, I realized how little we really knew about the people we were electing to the bench. That experience eventually led me to create LA Progressive's Judging the Judges series. Every election season, millions of Americans confront a familiar problem. They are asked to make decisions about candidates they know almost nothing about. Nowhere is this problem more apparent than in judicial elections. Most voters can tell you something about the candidates running for president, governor, or mayor. They may have heard them speak, watched them debate, or read about their positions on issues that matter to them. But when they reach the judicial contests on their ballots, the information often disappears. There are names. There are ballot designations. Occasionally, there are carefully crafted candidate statements. But there is precious little that tells voters how these individuals think, how they have exercised power, or what kind of judgment they bring to decisions that can alter people's lives. For years, I was one of those voters. I understood the importance of the judiciary. I understood that judges make consequential decisions about incarceration, family separation, housing, civil rights, and the application of the law. Yet when I looked at the judicial candidates on my ballot, I frequently knew almost nothing about them. Then something happened that changed my approach to judicial elections. Two Encounters With the Same Prosecutor More than a dozen years ago, I had been summoned for jury duty. During jury selection, I listened to a prosecutor whose presentation struck me as decidedly tough on crime. His tone and approach left an impression. Although I was not ultimately selected to serve on the jury, I remembered him. A short time later, I encountered that same prosecutor again. This time, he was running for a seat on the Los Angeles County Superior Court. He came to speak at my local Democratic club, an organization with a reputation for being a progressive bastion. What struck me was the contrast. The prosecutor I had observed during jury selection presented one face of himself in the courtroom. The judicial candidate standing before my fellow Democratic club members presented a decidedly different one. The courtroom prosecutor had emphasized a tough-on-crime approach. The candidate seeking the support of progressive voters sounded quite different. I couldn't ignore the disconnect. Perhaps both presentations reflected genuine aspects of his professional outlook. Prosecutors and judicial candidates operate in different settings, with different responsibilities. But the contrast raised a question I could not shake: How could voters know who they were really electing if they encountered candidates only in carefully managed campaign settings? My fellow club members had not necessarily seen what I had seen in that courtroom. They were evaluating the candidate based on his presentation to them. I had the unusual advantage of having observed him in a different professional setting. And it occurred to me that this was precisely the problem with judicial elections. Most voters never get to see candidates exercising the authority they already possess. They rarely observe them prosecuting cases, representing clients, ruling on motions, negotiating pleas, or interacting with the people whose lives are caught up in the justice system. Instead, voters encounter a campaign version of a professional whose record may be difficult to examine. That realization became the foundation of LA Progressive's Judging the Judges series. The Problem Isn't That Voters Don't Care I've been thinking a great deal about why Americans don't vote. Research shows that some nonvoters are discouraged by the available candidates, some believe their participation will make little difference, and others face practical barriers involving work, transportation, health, or family responsibilities. But there is another explanation that deserves greater attention: Sometimes people don't vote because they don't have enough information to make a responsible choice. Judicial elections illustrate that problem particularly well. When someone leaves a judicial contest blank, it's more likely than not that they don't know anything about the candidate. I understand that predicament because I experienced it myself. The distinction matters. If someone doesn't care about an election, persuading them to participate may require changing their sense of political engagement. But if someone wants to participate and lacks information, the immediate problem is different. They need access to credible, understandable research. That is a problem journalists can help address. Judicial Elections Demand More Than a Campaign Biography California's judicial elections are especially challenging. Superior Court judges serve six-year terms. Many first reach the bench through gubernatorial appointment, and uncontested incumbents generally do not appear on the ballot. When voters do face a contested judicial election, the candidates frequently have considerably lower public profiles than candidates for legislative or executive office. Yet the consequences of judicial decisions are anything but obscure. Judges decide whether people remain incarcerated while awaiting trial. They make rulings that can affect the admissibility of evidence, the conduct of criminal proceedings, child custody, civil disputes, and the protection of constitutional rights. Their work is not abstract. For someone facing the loss of freedom, housing, or family relationships, the person sitting on the bench can have an enormous impact. A judicial candidate's campaign presentation cannot tell us everything we need to know about how that person will exercise such authority. Neither can a résumé listing years of experience. Experience matters. Legal knowledge matters. Professional competence matters. But so do judicial temperament, fairness, impartiality, and a demonstrated commitment to applying the law faithfully. Those qualities deserve careful examination. Building Judging the Judges The experience with that prosecutor motivated me to begin researching judicial candidates rather than accepting the limited information placed before voters. That work developed into LA Progressive's Judging the Judges series. The series has appeared across multiple election cycles, with published installments dating back at least to 2008 and continuing through the 2026 elections. Over the years, our work has drawn on judicial candidate evaluations, public records, professional backgrounds, available interviews, and other sources that can help voters understand the people seeking seats on the bench. The goal has been to make judicial elections less mysterious. Research does not eliminate disagreement. Two informed people can review the same judicial candidate's record and reach different conclusions. And no amount of research can perfectly predict how someone will perform as a judge. But voters should not have to confront these elections armed with little more than a candidate's name and ballot designation. The public deserves accessible information about the professional experience, qualifications, and records of those seeking judicial authority. That belief continues to guide the series. What Voter Abstention Taught Me About Journalism The broader debate about voter participation has reinforced something I learned from that first experience. We often talk about voting as though the entire burden rests on the individual. Citizens are told that they have a responsibility to study the issues, research the candidates, and participate in elections. There is merit in that expectation. But what responsibility do our political institutions, news organizations, and civic associations bear for ensuring that meaningful information is available? Democracy asks citizens to exercise judgment. That judgment requires knowledge. And knowledge is not distributed equally. People with professional connections, legal expertise, flexible schedules, and access to political networks may have advantages in learning about candidates that other voters do not. Even someone who follows politics closely can struggle to find reliable information about judicial races. That information gap has consequences. When voters know little about the candidates, endorsements, ballot designations, name recognition, and campaign resources can assume greater importance. Those signals may provide useful information, but they are not substitutes for examining a candidate's professional record. This is also why I resist the easy characterization of nonvoters as apathetic. A voter who leaves a judicial race blank because the available information is inadequate has identified a real democratic problem. The answer cannot simply be to shame that person for not voting. We must also ask why such an important election presents such a difficult information challenge in the first place. From Frustration to Information I have never found a particularly convincing argument that simply staying home on Election Day will, by itself, improve our political system. I understand why people become frustrated. I understand why they lose confidence in candidates and institutions. And I understand why someone might refuse to cast a vote in a race where they cannot make an informed choice. But refusing to participate does not automatically produce a more accountable political system. Nor does casting an uninformed vote necessarily improve democracy. What I learned from my encounters with that prosecutor was that there is another response to the problem: investigate. Ask questions. Look beyond the campaign presentation. Examine the available record. Compare what candidates say with what they have actually done. Make the information accessible to others. That is what Judging the Judges grew out of. I did not begin researching judicial candidates because I believed I had all the answers. I began because I realized how much I didn't know. And because I had witnessed firsthand how differently the same candidate could present himself in a courtroom and before a room of progressive voters. That experience transformed a personal frustration into an ongoing publishing project. Years later, the lesson remains just as important. A democracy cannot reasonably expect informed participation while leaving voters uninformed about the people asking to exercise power over their lives. If we want to understand why people don't vote, we should certainly listen to their explanations. But we should also examine what we are asking them to do—and whether we have given them the tools to do it responsibly. For me, that inquiry began with jury duty, a prosecutor, and an unexpected second encounter at a Democratic club. It continues with every edition of Judging the Judges . California Judicial Elections: Research Resources These resources provide information about California Superior Court judicial candidates, including professional qualifications, disciplinary histories, courtroom conduct, campaign contributions, and voter guides. Los Angeles-specific sources are identified. Bar association evaluations and qualifications 1. Los Angeles County Bar Association (LACBA) — Judicial candidate evaluations and qualification ratings for Los Angeles Superior Court races. 2. State Bar of California — Attorney Search — Attorney licensing, years of practice, professional standing, and public disciplinary records. 3. State Bar — Judicial Nominees Evaluation Commission — Explains how candidates for gubernatorial judicial appointment are evaluated. Individual evaluations generally remain confidential. Judicial performance and courtroom conduct 4. The Robing Room — User-submitted reviews of judges, including California Superior Court judges. Reviews are anecdotal and should be independently verified. 5. California Commission on Judicial Performance — Official records of public judicial discipline and misconduct findings. 6. Los Angeles Superior Court — Judicial Officers — Current judicial assignments, departments, and courthouse information. 7. La Defensa — Court Watch LA — Courtroom accountability research, judicial observations, and judicial election materials. Court decisions and public records 8. California Courts — Judicial Opinions — Published appellate decisions, including decisions reviewing Superior Court rulings. 9. CourtListener — Searchable opinions and court records, including selected California cases. 10. Trellis Law — California trial court records, judicial rulings, and case information. Some features require payment. Campaign finance and candidate information 11. Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder — Official candidate information, election records, and voter information guides. 12. Los Angeles County Campaign Finance Portal — Judicial campaign contributions, expenditures, and financial disclosures. 13. California Secretary of State — Power Search — Searchable campaign finance information for committees filing at the state level. Many Superior Court campaigns file locally. California judicial election voter guides and reporting 14. LAist — 2026 Los Angeles Superior Court Judicial Guide — Candidate biographies, State Bar profiles, LACBA ratings, and candidate questionnaires. 15. LAist — How LACBA Evaluates Judicial Candidates — Explains the bar association's methodology and how to interpret its ratings. 16. La Defensa — November 2026 Voter Guide — Detailed research on Los Angeles Superior Court candidates, courtroom accountability, and the organization's endorsements. 17. Los Angeles Times — 2026 Superior Court Judicial Guide — Candidate experience, professional qualifications, and competitive judicial races. 18. articles.title: Turkey Risks Being Drawn Into Saudi Arabia’s War in Yemen
articles.author: Oğul Tuna
articles.content: There are few places outside Turkey that occupy such a mournful place in the country’s popular memory as Yemen. For generations, Turks who knew little about the politics of the Arabian Peninsula nevertheless knew Yemen through folk songs. They were ballads about young men sent from Anatolia to fight in Yemen, many of whom never returned. They told of mothers waiting for sons, women waiting for husbands, and a distant land associated above all with death. One of the most haunting was recorded by Ruhi Su, the great communist interpreter of Turkish folk music. Its refrain addresses the country with a bitter grandeur: Yemen, Yemen, glorious Yemen, Yemen, Yemen, your soil soaked in blood. The glory belonged to the empire. The dead belonged overwhelmingly to ordinary families. More than a century after the Ottoman withdrawal from Yemen, this old history has acquired an unexpected relevance. Turkey recently signed a new defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. As the regional war has spread to Saudi territory, Ankara has condemned Houthi attacks and has already begun providing Saudi Arabia with mainly defensive and technical support . As the fighting has escalated, the alliance has moved from planning toward implementation, while Turkish officials have begun openly discussing what further assistance Riyadh might require. Turkey is not at war in Yemen. But it has taken the first steps toward assuming obligations in a conflict that is not its own. The Turkish government and its allies would do well to remember one thing: Turks have been down this road before. The Empire Goes South The Ottoman presence in Yemen long predated the nineteenth century. But after the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 transformed the strategic importance of the Red Sea, Istanbul made a renewed effort to consolidate imperial control over the region, as a coalition of local tribes revolted in the 1870s. Among the officers sent south was Ahmed Muhtar Pasha. He would later become one of the Ottoman Empire’s most celebrated generals, particularly for his campaigns against the Russian army in 1877. But before earning fame on the Caucasian front, Muhtar Pasha served in Yemen, where Ottoman forces sought to extend Constantinople’s authority over territory that existed much more convincingly on imperial maps than it did on the ground. His memoirs describe the difficulties of campaigning through Yemen’s mountains and dealing with a political landscape structured by tribal loyalties, religious authority, local rivalries, and an unforgiving geography. Yes, the Ottoman army could capture towns. That did not mean the Ottoman state controlled the countryside around them. Military victories repeatedly failed to settle political questions. Rebellion was suppressed only to soon flare up again. More troops were dispatched. More money was spent. More men died. And the soldiers who bore this burden were generally not the men who had decided that Yemen was indispensable to the security of the empire. They were conscripts. That distinction, between those who define the strategic necessity of a war and those who actually pay for it, survived the Ottoman Empire itself. The generals and ministers disappeared. The popular memory remained, hence the songs. Saudi Arabia Learns the Same Lesson A century later, a vastly wealthier and technologically superior power encountered a variation of the same problem. When Saudi Arabia launched its military intervention in Yemen in 2015, there was little apparent symmetry between the two sides. Riyadh and its allies possessed modern aircraft, precision weapons, enormous financial resources, and crucial backing from the United States and other Western powers. Yet years of bombing failed to eliminate Ansar Allah, better known as the Houthis. The consequences for Yemen were catastrophic. Saudi Arabia’s US-backed campaign devastated civilian infrastructure and contributed to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. American and European arms manufacturers, meanwhile, profited from the weapons flowing toward the coalition. The Houthis have not only survived a decade of war but developed greater military capabilities than they began with. None of this makes Ansar Allah a progressive force. It remains, however, among the very few forces willing to confront American and Israeli military power directly — not merely rhetorically — and, in doing so, to challenge the US-led regional order. But there is equally little reason to accept the fantasy that military superiority allows an outside power to rearrange Yemen according to its wishes. The Ottomans learned this the hard way, and so did the Saudis after 2015. Turkey now risks stepping into the same political geography. A New Alliance On August 7, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, announcing that an armed attack against one member would be considered an attack against all three. Hakan Fidan compared the pledge to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s (NATO) Article 5. But in his account, assistance would follow a request from the threatened member and decisions by the relevant institutions; it would not automatically mean sending troops. He listed intelligence, logistics, ammunition, and potentially military units. Even Article 5 leaves NATO members discretion over how to assist an attacked ally. Ankara has made a commitment, but it still has choices. The pact also envisages cooperation before a crisis. On August 8, Fidan described plans for joint training and exercises, intelligence sharing, coordinated threat assessments, and cooperation in arms production. The aim is to make the three armed forces capable of operating together, with arrangements in place before a member calls for help. Some machinery is already taking shape. A committee of the three countries’ foreign and defense ministers and military chiefs met on August 31; a secretariat is planned in Riyadh. On September 19, Fidan said preparations for it and an associated military headquarters were nearly complete, but decisions on staffing and operations still lay in the future. NATO is the model, but this alliance is still being built. On September 18, the Financial Times reported that Turkish parliamentary ratification was still pending. Events have since moved considerably faster. On October 5, the three governments agreed to activate collective deterrence measures and prepare for the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in support of Saudi Arabia. Two days later, Turkish officials confirmed that Ankara had begun providing mainly defensive and technical assistance. Fidan has ruled out Turkish participation in offensive operations inside Yemen, but Ankara is considering air defense, electronic warfare, and other forms of military support. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has meanwhile said that the agreement will be submitted to parliament for ratification. Ankara insists the pact is defensive. But whose regional order might it defend? Iran’s setbacks in Syria and Lebanon have opened space for rival powers. Donald Trump has publicly welcomed the agreement. One possible outcome is, in effect, a division of labor: Israel attacks Iran and its allies, while US-aligned regional powers expand their influence at Tehran’s expense. Their rivalry with Israel could coexist with policies that reinforce an order favorable to Washington. The NATO analogy would then extend to the consolidation of a US-led order beyond the promise of mutual defense. The pact’s immediate test, however, is in Yemen. Renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi territory and Riyadh’s military response are now testing what its promises mean in practice. The pressure is, however, no longer coming from Riyadh alone. On October 13, Trump publicly suggested that he might ask Erdoğan to help Saudi Arabia against the Houthis. Turkey is thus confronted not with an abstract treaty provision but with the possibility that its new ally might request assistance during an actual war. On September 19, Fidan addressed precisely that possibility. He condemned attacks against Saudi sovereignty and territorial integrity and said that Riyadh might have military requirements, particularly of a technical nature. Under the new agreement, he indicated, Turkey would have no problem meeting such needs. “Technical” no longer describes merely a hypothetical form of assistance. Turkey has already begun providing mainly defensive and technical support to Saudi Arabia. Intelligence and logistical support can help sustain a military campaign without a single Turkish battalion entering Yemen. Deeper involvement would still require further decisions. But each commitment can give Ankara another reason to make the next one. Whose War Is It? There is a deeper contradiction in Ankara’s position. Fidan has simultaneously argued that Saudi Arabia should not be dragged into the confrontation between the United States and Iran. Turkey has called for diplomacy and attempted to present itself as an actor capable of communicating with the different sides. But if Saudi Arabia should not be dragged into someone else’s war, the same question must surely be asked of Turkey. The present regional conflagration was not initiated by an attack on Turkey. Turkish territory is not under Houthi occupation. The Turkish people have no dispute with the people of Yemen. The current regional escalation has grown out of the US-Israeli confrontation with Iran and the network of alliances surrounding it. Ansar Allah has positioned itself firmly on Tehran’s side of that struggle. Saudi Arabia, willingly or not, has become another arena in it. Now the pact gives Riyadh a basis for seeking Turkish help and Ankara a reason to treat Saudi security as its own. That does not make intervention inevitable. It makes refusing further involvement a political choice that the language of alliance solidarity can make harder to defend. The Turkish government may believe that its increasingly close military relationship with Riyadh increases Ankara’s regional influence. Turkey’s defense industry may also find new opportunities in Saudi demand for drones, missiles, electronic warfare systems, and other military technology. But what appears from Ankara as strategic influence looks rather different from below. There is no single “regional interest” at stake here. The Saudi monarchy and the Turkish state are pursuing their own interests, as are Washington and Israel in their confrontation with Iran, and Ansar Allah and Tehran on the other side. Defense contractors have interests of a more profitable kind. The people who die in these struggles rarely have much say in defining any of them. The Price of “National Interest” This is where the Ottoman experience matters. Not because Erdoğan is some latter-day sultan, as he is still too often caricatured in the Western press. Nor because modern Turkey is the Ottoman Empire, or because every Turkish move in the region can be explained away as “neo-Ottomanism.” And not because twenty-first-century Yemen is identical to the Yemen encountered by Ahmed Muhtar Pasha. Such analogies explain very little. The continuity lies elsewhere. States have always been extraordinarily good at converting the interests of rulers, strategic establishments, and economic elites into something called the “national interest.” Once that transformation has been accomplished, ordinary people can be asked to sacrifice themselves for objectives they had no role in determining. Ottoman officials had perfectly sophisticated strategic arguments for holding Yemen. Control of the Red Sea mattered. Rival European empires mattered. The security of the holy cities mattered. Imperial prestige mattered. None of these arguments made the dead conscript less dead. Today, the vocabulary has changed. Politicians and pundits say that regional security and alliance credibility and defense cooperation matter, or that Turkey’s influence in the Persian Gulf matters. Maritime trade matters. But before accepting these abstractions as reasons to go to war, there is a more elementary question: Who benefits, and who pays? Turkey’s rapidly expanding arms industry would certainly benefit from deeper military cooperation with the Gulf monarchies. Political elites may benefit from the prestige of projecting Turkish power beyond the country’s borders. The young soldier ordered to defend that projection will experience it differently. So will the Yemeni family living underneath the drones. Yemen, Yemen . . . The Ottoman Empire eventually disappeared from Yemen. The official case for holding Yemen has largely faded from popular memory. The officials who sent troops south are remembered mostly by specialists. Many of the battles mean almost nothing to modern Turks. Yet the songs survived. That should tell us something about how war enters popular memory. The state remembers campaigns, commanders, and victories. Ordinary people remember the son who did not return. Ruhi Su understood the difference. When he sang the old Yemen songs, he was not celebrating imperial strategy. His voice belonged to another tradition, one that preserved the suffering concealed beneath the language of glory. That is why an Ottoman general’s memoir and a communist folk singer unexpectedly belong in the same story. Ahmed Muhtar Pasha shows us the view from the campaign, while Ruhi Su gives us the view from home. Between them lies the history that Ankara should remember before “technical assistance” becomes something larger. Turkey has no need to return to Yemen. Its people have already paid for that lesson once before. Yemen, Yemen, glorious Yemen, Yemen, Yemen, your soil soaked in blood. articles.title: Client Lifecycle Management
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Financial institutions manage client relationships through onboarding, verification, account servicing, reviews, and closure. Each stage creates tasks, decisions, records, and compliance obligations that require consistent handling. When teams manage these activities separately, information becomes fragmented, and delays increase. That is where a structured, end-to-end process adds the most value. Client lifecycle management connects the full relationship into one structured process, giving teams clearer ownership, better data, and stronger oversight. The approach becomes easier to understand by examining its main stages and practical value. Here is a closer look at what the process involves and the problems it helps solve. What Client Lifecycle Management Covers Client onboarding begins when a prospective client enters the organization’s pipeline. The process captures identity details, business information, ownership structures, risk factors, and required documentation during client lifecycle management. This structure connects onboarding with later verification, due diligence, monitoring, review, and closure tasks, so teams maintain a consistent record throughout the relationship. Know Your Customer checks and identity verification confirm who the client is. Due diligence then assesses factors such as ownership, location, products requested, and expected activity. The depth of review depends on the client’s risk profile and applicable compliance requirements. After onboarding, the relationship requires ongoing attention. Teams update client information, conduct periodic reviews, monitor transactions, manage documentation, and respond to changes in ownership or risk. The lifecycle ends when the institution closes the relationship and records the required offboarding actions. A structured process connects these activities through shared information and defined workflows. Instead of asking different teams to collect the same details repeatedly, the institution reuses approved data across relevant tasks. That structure reduces avoidable handoffs and gives staff a clearer record of what happened, when it happened, and who approved it. Why It Matters A well-structured lifecycle process delivers measurable improvements in three key areas. Faster, More Consistent Onboarding Client onboarding often involves relationship managers, compliance specialists, operations teams, and clients. Without coordinated workflows, each group may request information through separate channels, creating delays and duplicate work. A lifecycle process assigns tasks based on client type, risk level, product, and jurisdiction. Straightforward cases follow a defined route, while higher-risk cases receive additional review. Teams spend less time sorting requests and more time resolving issues that require judgment. Consistency also improves the client experience. Clients receive clearer requests, fewer repeated questions, and better visibility into outstanding requirements. Better Compliance Control Compliance depends on accurate information, complete records, and timely reviews. A fragmented process makes it harder to confirm whether teams followed the right policy for each client. Lifecycle management places rules and approval steps inside operational workflows. The process records submitted documents, verification results, risk assessments, review dates, and decisions. Managers gain a clearer audit trail, while compliance teams can identify overdue actions before they become larger problems. This control matters because client risk changes after onboarding. A change in ownership, unusual transaction activity, or a new regulatory requirement can affect the relationship. The institution needs ongoing due diligence that supports action throughout the client’s tenure, not only during account opening. Lower Operating Costs Repeated data entry creates unnecessary work and increases the chance of errors. Staff members also lose time searching across email threads, spreadsheets, shared drives, and separate systems. A connected process gives approved client information a usable home. Integrations then move relevant data between systems without requiring manual copying at every step. Fewer handoffs reduce processing time and limit corrections caused by inconsistent records. The financial effect extends beyond labor. Better data quality reduces rework, supports faster decisions, and helps teams manage larger client volumes without matching increases in administrative effort. What a Strong Process Requires A useful lifecycle process starts with clear ownership. Every task should have an assigned team, a defined deadline, and an escalation route when information is missing or risk changes. Data standards matter just as much. Institutions need consistent client fields, document requirements, risk categories, and review triggers. Without shared standards, automation only moves inconsistent information faster. Integration is also necessary. Client lifecycle management works best when onboarding, identity verification, Know Your Customer checks, transaction monitoring, and account records exchange relevant data. Staff should see the information needed for a decision without rebuilding the client record manually. Finally, reporting should show more than completed tasks. Managers need visibility into bottlenecks, aging cases, exception volumes, review backlogs, and recurring documentation problems. These measures help teams correct process weaknesses with evidence rather than assumptions. Conclusion Client lifecycle management gives financial institutions a structured way to manage relationships after the initial application. It connects onboarding, verification, due diligence, monitoring, reviews, and offboarding through shared data and assigned workflows. The practical next step is to map every client touchpoint, identify repeated requests, and record where ownership becomes unclear. That review creates a concrete basis for improving process design, selecting supporting technology, and measuring better operational control.

articles.title: It Won’t Stop With Ilhan Omar
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: Up until now, the Donald Trump-J. D. Vance administration has been busy weaponizing the US immigration system against fairly low-level political opponents: college students protesting US support for Israel’s genocide, independent journalists applying scrutiny to government policies, or random tourists who happened to be critical of the president and his lackeys. Now it’s taking the unprecedented step of turning it against a sitting member of Congress. The federal raid on Squad member Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home carried out earlier this week has now all but officially been confirmed to be an immigration-related investigation trying to strip her of US citizenship and deport her, as sources separately relayed to Fox News , the New York Post , the Washington Post , and the Wall Street Journal . It is just the latest and most extreme case of Trump and his people using the US immigration system and the massive bureaucracy that exists to enforce it as a vehicle for political repression based on a thinly veiled excuse. There’s little doubt this is politically motivated. It’s not just that Omar has already been investigated for this with no charges to show for it, that this immigration history has been a right-wing media obsession for years, or that Trump and his underlings — who have turned the Department of Justice into the president’s personal vehicle for score-settling on his many grudges — have singled out Omar as a target for the better part of a decade, often by flinging around wild and unproven accusations about her immigration history and repeatedly threatening to deport her. It’s clearly politically motivated because they’ve been openly saying they would do exactly what is happening now. Besides Trump’s constant threats to deport her, the wife of one of Trump’s top advisers, Stephen Miller, reacted to the news of the raid by tweeting , “Promise made, promise kept,” before swiftly deleting it. Vice President Vance declared seven months ago that Omar “definitely committed immigration fraud.” Vance is now saying that the White House isn’t involved and that they simply want “to let the law, the facts drive this” — but immediately undercut this cleanup attempt by then railing against Omar for “hav[ing] such disdain and such rage at the country that gave her a better life,” before reminding the interviewer they would “follow the law” if they discovered a crime. They get so excited at the idea of deporting one of their fiercest critics that they can’t help themselves. To put it plainly, Trump and company long ago decided that Omar is guilty of whatever they’re going to accuse her of and that she should be exiled from her country. This raid and whatever investigation comes of it is, to them, just a formality. No administration in modern memory has targeted a congressperson like this, and certainly not with weeks to go before she’s up for reelection — since a criminal investigation, which may not even result in charges, let alone any guilty verdict, has the obvious potential to be a politically damaging “October surprise” (even if it ends up being completely free of substance). The fact that they’re carrying out this unprecedented move is a major escalation of two separate Trump-Vance administration policies. One is its transformation of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in particular, into a tool for intimidating the many swaths of the country that do not like the president or his sidekick. (The raid was conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, a branch of ICE.) That approach has seen ICE kill at least three US citizens and many more noncitizens as well as illegally detain hundreds of citizens and deport around a dozen of them. The less-well-known policy is the administration’s push to turbocharge denaturalizations, which are now at unheard-of levels . The administration has eagerly publicized the cases where this has been aimed at violent criminals convicted for heinous crimes. But given that the investigation into Omar is being done with an eye to denaturalizing her, too, it raises the question of how many of these other denaturalization cases may be similarly politically driven. It’s worth remembering at this point that Vance gave his personal endorsement to a book that called for weaponizing the immigration system against the Right’s political adversaries in exactly this way, with the Red Scares of last century as its model. Ironically, as the Trump-Vance administration accelerates its preplanned crackdown on the Left, it’s nakedly letting literally scores of right-wing criminals off the hook for their offenses. A Reuters report earlier this week revealed how the White House has turned the presidential pardon into a system of personal patronage, trading clemency and a clean slate for past crimes for favors, which eighty-five mostly conservatives have benefited from so far — including a former Republican official who fundraised off of a dead police officer, then used the proceeds to buy herself plastic surgery and other goodies. It also mirrors the Trump-Vance administration’s policy toward Latin America. There it has freed a right-wing former president convicted of drug trafficking and otherwise politically gotten into bed with local alleged narcotraffickers while at the same time abducting a a left-wing leader on drug-trafficking charges , fueling a crackdown on other left-leaning officials in the region on similar grounds, and carrying out a campaign of indiscriminate murder in international waters on the basis of stopping the drug trade (which it has miserably failed at actually doing). This is the Trump-Vance ethos in a nutshell: maximum pressure and punishment for political opponents spuriously accused of crimes and maximum leniency for actual criminals who happen to be the duo’s political allies. There is one more thing to say about this, which is that everything laid out here is, sadly, not the unique behavior of two particularly power-hungry right-wing officials in the United States. This is just arguably the most extreme instance of what has now become shamefully standard across Western democracies, whether governed by liberals or conservatives: of using the immigration system as a way to punish and silence individuals whose speech those in power disagree with, since immigration systems have a variety of legal loopholes and few to no real constitutional protections. Look at what happened just this past week. Russian journalist and exiled Vladimir Putin critic Leonid Ragozin was officially notified that he was being expelled from Latvia, which he called home for more than a decade, by government decree — explicitly because of his critical reporting on the European role in the war in Ukraine, and likely also as belated political reprisal for years-old reporting that embarrassed the Latvian political elite. Meanwhile, former British diplomat Ian Proud was detained for hours at Heathrow airport and treated like a criminal — searched, fingerprints and DNA taken, electronics seized — under a recently passed (by the Labour government) anti-terrorism statute, all for the crime of having visited Russia to attend a conference. Remember when Vance, at the beginning of his tenure, did a long, pompous speech tut-tutting European officials for being hostile to “the idea that somebody with an alternative viewpoint might express a different opinion” and reminding them that “there is no security if you are afraid of the voices, the opinions and the conscience that guide your very own people”? And European officials responded with indignation that anyone would deign to dress them down on this subject? Less than two years later, it’s hard to know which of them was the bigger hypocrite — or even which of the two places Vance was describing in his speech. articles.title: Sons of Vietnamese Refugees
articles.author: Reia Li
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. California has just a handful of truly competitive congressional races this year, as a nationwide redistricting battle and a new map approved under Gov. Gavin Newsom’s Proposition 50 have reshaped the electoral landscape. The tightest contests are in the Central Valley and San Diego County, but the fight also extends to Orange County, a onetime Republican stronghold where Democratic Rep. Derek Tran is defending his seat. This year marks the first time two Vietnamese Americans are running to represent the district, which includes Little Saigon, the largest concentration of people of Vietnamese ancestry outside of Vietnam. Roughly 13% of the district’s population is Vietnamese, according to Census Bureau data. Tran and his Republican challenger Chuong Vo are both children of Vietnamese refugees who fled after the Fall of Saigon in the 1970s. Both grew up in households that relied on public assistance, but they draw very different lessons from that experience, which is reflected in their approach to policy. Tran opposed Republican cuts to government assistance programs under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act , while Vo touts the benefits of President Donald Trump’s signature legislation, which included trillions of dollars in tax cuts over the next decade. “Thank God for the Big Beautiful Bill this year because I don’t know about you, but I got some money back for the first time ever,” Vo told supporters at a Gardena restaurant in April. In an interview with Capital & Main, Vo attributed his family’s success to hard work combined with government support when they needed a bit of help. “When I was young, my whole family was on welfare. Of course, we were refugees. We came here with nothing,” Vo said. “But we made sure that we got off the system.” The contest reflects a familiar ideological divide between Democrats and Republicans, but it is unfolding against an especially aggressive attack on the safety net. H.R. 1, or the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, partially paid for tax breaks by slashing over $1 trillion from social programs, including Medicaid and food assistance. As a result of those cuts, an estimated 44,008 people in the district could lose health insurance by 2034, according to an analysis by the Joint Economic Committee in Congress . Refugees — as both candidates’ parents once were — are no longer eligible for Medicaid or SNAP benefits funded with federal money (although California will continue to fund Medi-Cal , the state’s version of Medicaid, for some immigrants). To Tran, who voted against H.R. 1 , the cuts serve as a reminder of his own former reliance on government support. “I grew up on those safety net programs that the Republicans are trying to cut, whether it’s WIC [the nutrition program for low-income women and children], whether it’s Section 8 housing, you know, food stamps. That was my childhood, because that was what was required for us to be able to survive in this country, right?” Tran told volunteers during a campaign event in Garden Grove on Sept. 26. Over a third of District 45 residents rely on Medi-Cal, according to 2025 data from the California Health Care Foundation . More than one in 10 rely on SNAP, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture . In the Vietnamese community in particular, many have depended on social welfare programs , said Bich-Tram Le, an anchor and news commentator at Orange County’s largest Vietnamese-language news source, Nguoi Viet. Almost 80% of Vietnamese immigrants in the U.S. are citizens, but among Vietnamese households led by a noncitizen, 47% rely on one or more welfare programs, the highest rate among Asian immigrant households, according to a 2026 report by the Center for Immigration Studies. “People in our community will get hurt because of those cuts,” Le said. Despite Vo’s public support for H.R. 1, his campaign website says that he will vote to “protect Social Security and Medicare for today’s seniors.” He told Capital & Main that he sees those programs as distinct from income-targeted public assistance programs because workers contribute to them. “Social Security is an earned benefit,” Vo said. “It shouldn’t be given to those that didn’t earn it.” The 45th Congressional District was solidly Republican since its creation in 1983. That changed, however, in 2018, when voters elected a Democrat for the first time. Since then, voters have swung back and forth between red and blue when selecting their representative in the House. Most of District 45 is in Orange County, but it also includes a small corner of southeast L.A. County. In the redrawn district, 38.6% of registered voters are Democrats and 30.4% are Republicans, according to the California Secretary of State’s Office . The remaining 31% of voters are either independents or have no party affiliation. Those are the voters Chuong and Vo are courting. James Syto, 59, is an independent voter in Santa Ana. Syto said he works 16-hour days as a caregiver. He earns too much to qualify for Medi-Cal, but not enough to be able to comfortably afford his health care premiums and rent. He makes weekly visits to a food pantry in Santa Ana to supplement groceries for his family. When he votes in November, food prices and access to health care will be on his mind. “Medi-Cal and groceries in the market: That’s the main problem,” Syto said. Vo, following a familiar Republican playbook, has painted his opponent as a socialist. Vo points to Tran’s vote against a House resolution that condemned “socialism in all forms” on Sept. 1. Tran defended his decision by saying that Republicans rejected his proposal to amend the bill to include language specifically denouncing the Communist government in Vietnam, according to a press release. The labels of socialist or Communist have particular emotional weight for some older Vietnamese immigrants, who fled North Vietnamese Communist forces decades ago. “We remember that because that’s our pain. That’s our historic pain,” said Brandon Bui, 54, a Garden Grove resident who, on a recent Saturday, came to a neighborhood park where Vo was hosting a campaign event. Bui said that he associates the Democratic Party with socialism, especially as candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America appear on the November ballot. “They’ve got socialists running. They could do something to stop that. Why wouldn’t they?” Bui said, referring to the Democratic Party. Of course, Tran also has his supporters in the Vietnamese community. Cai Le, 70, joined a volunteer canvass just a couple of miles away from Vo’s campaign event in Garden Grove. She was part of a small group of Vietnamese-speaking volunteers specifically targeting members of her community. “I want the government to take care of poor people,” Le said. Tran has not only received criticism from the right. Among some younger, progressive voters, Tran’s record on immigration has been disappointing, said Tracy La, the executive director of VietRISE, a nonprofit advocating for Vietnamese and other immigrant communities in Orange County. Last year, Tran voted for the Laken-Riley Act, which mandated detentions for certain immigrants arrested or charged with certain crimes. Opponents of the measure argue that it violates migrants’ due process rights, since they could be detained, even if they are never convicted of a crime. “It’s especially frustrating because both these candidates are campaigning on the immigrant story yet again,” La said. “But they’re not using it to connect with the realities of what their constituents are facing.” The majority-minority district’s population is 39% Asian and 35% Latino. During the summer of 2025, arrests by ICE increased sevenfold in the agency’s “area of responsibility” in Southern California, which includes Orange County, according to data provided by ICE in response to the Deportation Data Project and analyzed by Capital & Main. Tran is approaching Election Day with several advantages over his opponent. Prop. 50 redrew his district, making it about five percentage points more Democratic. What’s more, a majority of U.S. adults disapprove of Trump’s handling of tariffs, the war in Iran and the cost of living, according to a late September poll from the Associated Press-NORC . Trump’s approval rating stands at 37%, per an average of national polls . Despite the political tailwinds for Tran, the seat is still not a safe one for the incumbent, according to the Cook Political Report . This race is a bellwether for Democratic candidates’ prospects nationwide, said Steve Barkan, a Democratic political consultant. “If the Democrats don’t win this, then I don’t think there’s much of a chance that they would take back the House,” Barkan said.
