articles.title: How Israel Controls Palestinian Land
articles.author: Vijay Prashad
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Israel’s genocidal bombing campaign has devastated Gaza’s wastewater system, destroying or damaging nearly 90% of the territory’s water and sanitation infrastructure since 2023. Every day, 45,000 cubic metres of untreated sewage are discharged into the Mediterranean Sea while an additional 15,000 cubic metres seep into the ground. This collapse of sanitation infrastructure has led to an infestation of rats and other rodents in Gaza, with two in three children living in displacement sites plagued by these vermin. In September 2026, an exceptional algal bloom clogged filtration systems at five of Israel’s six desalination plants, with the Israeli environmental group Zalul warning that untreated sewage from Gaza was contributing to the worsening crisis. As you sow, so shall you reap. Majdal Nateel (Palestine), Studying the Void of Amputation , 2025. A ceasefire does not rebuild a home. In Gaza, Palestinians still live among the ruins of Israel’s campaign of mass killing and destruction. A year after the ceasefire took effect, hundreds of thousands remain in worn-out tents, temporary shelters, and damaged buildings. The halt in major fighting has not even restored the basic conditions in which people can live with dignity. The destruction in Gaza cannot be captured by data alone, though numbers do give a sense of the scale of the devastation wrought by Israel and its allies. For instance, a recent UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) report found that 92% of Gaza’s economic establishments had been destroyed or damaged. In 2025, real GDP per person was $212, just 17% of its already low 2022 level, and more than 90% of Gaza’s working-age population was without employment. By May 2026, just $17 billion had been pledged towards the estimated $71.5 billion cost of Gaza’s recovery and reconstruction and only a small fraction of the pledged funds had been disbursed. Gaza will remain a ruin for some time yet to come. Juhaina Habibi Kandalaft (Palestine), Ardi, biti (My Home, My Land), 2015. Families in Gaza who have lived in tents for over two years report that their living spaces are so cramped that every aspect of family life – from conversation and cooking to sleeping and bathing – takes place without privacy. A mapping exercise by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) of more than 500 displacement sites found that only about half were within 500 metres of a safe space for women and girls. As of late July 2026, 17 such spaces remained closed for lack of funding and two more for security reasons, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs . Psychosocial specialist Abeer al-Shurafa told al-Araby al-Jadeed that ‘the closely stuck tents leave people’s lives exposed to others and create conditions that encourage prying, interference in family affairs, and eavesdropping on conversations. Many of the problems that now exist between families are directly linked to this imposed reality. The absence of privacy affects the upbringing of children and relations between spouses and may contribute to an increase in family disputes and divorce rates because what once took place inside the home now happens in an exposed space where others can hear it’. UNFPA reported that between April and June 2026, cases of gender-based violence recorded by ten case-management partners rose 27% compared with the previous quarter. The three most commonly reported forms of violence – denial of resources, psychological and emotional violence, and physical assault – each accounted for roughly one third of reported cases while forced and early marriage accounted for 2.6%. These figures cannot be separated from the material conditions created by Israel’s assault on Gaza. The destruction of homes, property, and livelihoods, together with the breakdown of family and social support under displacement, has made women more dependent on aid agencies and men in their families for food, water, shelter, and income. Haya Kaabneh (Palestine), The Mourning of Spring , 2024. Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank Israeli forces demolish Palestinian homes and Zionist settlers drive communities from land that their families have inhabited for generations. This displacement is not an accident. In January and February 2025, Israeli forces entered the Palestinian refugee camps in Jenin, Nur Shams, and Tulkarem, forcibly displaced their populations, and destroyed hundreds of homes, roads, and other civilian infrastructure. The roughly 33,000 expelled Palestinians remain barred from returning. Related: Netanyahu’s Empty Seats and the Business of Occupation In February 2026, after years of attacks and harassment, Israeli settlers forced the 45 members of a Bedouin herding community out of al-Wadi al-Shamali, north of al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya in the occupied West Bank. The expulsion left the valley without a Palestinian presence, enabling settlers to extend their control over grazing land and threatening some 2,000 dunams of surrounding farmland, including olive groves. This seizure, along with Israeli plans to build thousands of illegal settlement units in the E1 area near Jerusalem, undermines the territorial basis of a future Palestinian state. Ismail Fattah (Iraq), Untitled, 1994. Less often discussed is the economic stranglehold that Israel exercises over the occupied Palestinian territory. According to the UNCTAD report , the Israeli government deducted or withheld more than $3.67 billion in Palestinian revenues between January 2019 and March 2026. Palestinian dependence extends into the currency itself. Much of the income earned by Palestinians enters Palestinian banks in Israeli shekels. But Israel limits how much physical cash those banks can return to Israel’s banking system. Data from the Palestine Economic Policy Research Institute (MAS) show that between 2021 and 2024, the permitted transfers did not keep pace with the volume of cash that required repatriation. The resulting surplus fills bank vaults with money that cannot readily be lent or used to settle payments, leading some banks to restrict new shekel deposits. The MAS study cites an IMF estimate that the cost of holding this surplus reduced Palestinian banks’ profits by about 20%. Trapping this cash in Palestinian bank vaults creates more than an awkward pile of banknotes. Payments to suppliers depend on a functional correspondent banking link with Israeli banks. A breakdown of this system could disrupt imports of electricity, fuel, and water. In August 2026, Israel agreed to bring forward the fourth-quarter shipment of 4.5 billion shekels, easing the immediate pressure. But discretionary shipments do not end a system in which Israel determines whether Palestinian banks can process payments in the currency on which much of the Palestinian economy depends. Electronic payments may slow cash accumulation, MAS argues, but they cannot remove that structural constraint. Ismail Shammout (Palestine), Untitled , 1994. Israel is not the only beneficiary of this policy of apartheid, strangulation, and expropriation. On 25 September 2026, the UN Human Rights Office updated its database of enterprises involved in specified activities linked to Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem. The updated list includes companies based in France (Egis and Egis Rail), Germany (Heidelberg Materials AG), the Netherlands (Booking.com), and the United States (Airbnb, Booking Holdings, Expedia Group, and Tripadvisor). The report identifies activities such as services that sustain settlements and the commercial exploitation of land or other natural resources. It assesses different forms of corporate involvement, including contribution and direct linkage, rather than making a criminal finding about every firm. These are familiar names because settlement commerce is folded into ordinary consumer and business infrastructure: a holiday listing, a transport service, a quarry product. The database is explicitly limited to settlement-related activities: it is neither a census of every company profiting from the occupation nor the end of the inquiry into those it names. The UN Human Rights Office asks states to regulate businesses under their jurisdiction and calls on companies to prevent or address adverse human rights impacts. The question for Western governments is concrete: will they let companies registered at home continue to provide the services and material connections that enable the settlements? Fateh Moudarres (Syria), Alm (Pain), 1961. While writing this newsletter, I came across ‘Nablus Street’ by the journalist and poet Mustafa Abu Sneineh in an anthology of contemporary Palestinian verse. The poem seethes with frustration at apartheid, genocide, and expropriation. Ordinary life rubs against these ugly phenomena. It was a wordless confession. I recall the sun sliding into the darkness of the settlement, Soldiers with guns beating the sunset until it passed out. A lovestruck boy stealing poems from Nizar Qabbani and love letters from The Snow Comes Through the Window. I’m still a lovestruck boy Even though the sun has long since gone under Even though my first confession of love Was made in the crosshairs of the occupation’s guns. I want to walk on Nablus Street with you too and to read Hanna Mina’s The Snow Comes Through the Window (1969). Mina, who was born in Syria, worked as a barber and distributed the Communist newspaper Sawt al-Shaab (Voice of the People) on the streets. His novel follows Fayyad, a leftist writer who flees to Lebanon to escape political persecution. It is the story of a sensitive man who moves from private fear to collective struggle. The soldiers in the poem beat the sunset, but the next day, the sun rises and brightens the sky. Tricontinental

articles.title: Women Politicians Under Attack
articles.author: Steven Hill
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Bernadet Greene-Placentia, the Democratic candidate for Arizona’s 8th Congressional District, claimed a week ago that she was struck in the head, knocked unconscious and raped by two men while she was repairing one of her campaign signs. Greene-Placentia, who is no shrinking violet having worked as a long-haul trucker and small business owner, filed an official incident report with the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office (MCSO), but didn’t do so until 17 days after the alleged event occurred. Due to that delay, some are doubting her story , calling it a publicity stunt to boost her campaign in a Republican-leaning district. But according to the police report, Greene-Placentia sustained several documented injuries, including a bump on her head , finger-type bruising on her arms, and bruises on her flank. She told investigators that one of the men said “Democratic bitch” at some point during the attack. She has explained that her reasons for not immediately reporting to the police or undergoing a sexual assault medical forensic exam was due to her trauma, shock, embarrassment and self-shaming, and not wanting the incident to distract from her campaign. She says she just wanted to “bury it.” So the debate rages, even as the sheriff’s office continues to investigate, with no suspects so far publicly identified or charged. However this case turns out, the truth is, Bernadet Greene-Placentia is not the only woman candidate or politician who has reported claims of physical violence, harassment and/or intimidation. Her story is yet another example illustrating a disturbing and broader pattern: over the last several years, a national and even global backlash against women’s political rise has been rearing its ugly head. Women elected officials are being intimidated, harassed and threatened in growing and alarming numbers. And authoritarian leaders like Donald Trump, Argentina’s Javier Milei and Brazil’s jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro have led the way in fomenting this hostile climate, using digital media and public statements as primary weapons in their arsenal. Related: Why Are Democrats Shooting Themselves in the Foot on Ranked Choice Voting? Reality rearing its ugly head A study by the Brennan Center found that women holding state and local office in the US were three to four times as likely as men to experience gender-based abuse; and women state legislators were nearly four times as likely as men to experience abuse of a sexual nature. Moreover, women as well as people of color legislators reported experiencing more severe and threatening forms of abuse than their male or white respondents. In interviews, one female state legislator related her experience of strangers “identifying my address or talking about my daughter or my mom or, you know, making overt rape or death threats. . . . My husband just showed me a thread on Reddit yesterday about people talking about — men — what they would do to me. And we women just sort of have to compartmentalize it.” Another female legislator said of her harassers, “They don’t directly say, ‘I’m going to kill her children.’ But they’ll make comments like, ‘We’re going to take over her home. Here’s the address. Here’s a photo of it. She lives here in [town], but her kids don’t go to school [in town] — they go in [neighboring town].’” A female state representative from Texas, said, “Sometimes we’re on the legislative ﬂoor, and in the galleries above us there are people who are armed. And especially when we’re having those controversial debates, I’m thinking, ‘God, one person. It just takes one person.’ We’re like sitting ducks. I’m still going to do what I’m going to do as far as legislating. But I’m not naive enough to think it could never happen to us.” In the past, high profile attacks against women leaders have set the nation on edge. In June 2025, a gunman assassinated former Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband. Who can forget the brutal shooting and near-murder of Congresswoman Gabby Giffords outside a supermarket where the congresswoman was meeting with constituents in Tucson AZ. Or the attempted kidnapping of Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer in 2020, and the hammer attack on Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s husband by a right-wing zealot looking for the Speaker in her San Francisco home. Male political leaders have also been targeted for political violence, including President Donald Trump and right-wing activist Charlie Kirk. Yet evidence shows that women politicians face unique and pervasive harms. In one national safety survey, 93% of women legislator respondents reported experiencing some form of abuse or harassment as legislators. Harm often manifests on a day-to-day basis as sexualized threats , professional dismissal or appearance-based insults. Not surprisingly, women in ofﬁce, and especially women of color, report having to take extra time and adopt special tactics to stay safe. Women state legislators are nearly twice as likely as men to change their travel routes because of abuse concerns, and more than six times as likely as men to avoid traveling alone. Fifty-ﬁve percent of women of color legislators said they avoid traveling alone. And nearly half of women officeholders said they were less willing to run for reelection or higher office because of the shocking levels of threats and abuse. This is serious, Taliban-like stuff. Another study found that female mayors are more likely than men to experience physical violence, harassment and psychological abuse, and those who suffered physical violence were more likely to have considered ending their political careers. A separate study by the same researchers concluded that women state senators with higher levels of power (party or committee leaders) were more likely than other women to experience psychological abuse and sexualized abuse and violence; Democratic women state senators faced more sexualized abuse and violence than Republican women. Another study found that, among congressional candidates, women of color were most likely to experience sexist, racist and violent abuse online. Related: From “11,780 Votes” to Trump’s 2026 Election Power Grab The role of digital media in attacks on women leaders An important and often overlooked component of the backlash is the way that the internet and digital media platforms have turbocharged these harms. These increasingly dominant communication tools are providing a global platform to bad actors intent on doing bad things to their targeted victims. This is much more than simply the continuation of sexism by other means. These are potent communication technologies that have unleashed the worst impulses of the worst specimens of humanity, and allowed them to find each other anywhere in the world, and encourage, strategize and share tactics together. Male extremist groups like the Proud Boys and Boogaloo Bois right-wing militias congregate in clandestine Facebook Groups that can be walled off as “hidden” or secret and accessible only to admitted members. Other secret meet-ups on the internet can be found on platforms like subReddits, Parler, Signal, Telegram, WhatsApp, and chat rooms on 4chan and 8kun. Some of these are encrypted against unauthorized entry into private groups, including by law enforcement. In their digital lairs, participants have circulated links to manuals on bomb construction, kidnapping, making flash stun grenades , snipers, and murder. Some of these groups have had thousands of members . In years past, if you were the only person in your geographic area who had extremist views, organizing with other like-minded but geographically dispersed extremists was costly and logistically difficult. Now, the use of digital media drastically reduces these costs and allows such individuals to find each other more easily to organize and collaborate. These online forums – kind of like hidden “digital hideouts” - are filled with men of all ages concealed behind the anonymity of the internet. Inside their digital Fight Club of fury they can easily direct their bitter hostility at their chosen targets of women in general, and female elected leaders in particular. These “het-bro” digital hideouts are now increasingly accompanied by other technologies, such as self-learning artificial intelligence and highly realistic immersive technologies, resulting in a proliferation in the production of deepfakes, the vast majority of which are imitative pornography videos featuring the likenesses of real women. Fake nude images have spread all over the internet, increasing by 290 percent in recent years. Linda Robinson, a senior fellow for Women and Foreign Policy at the Council on Foreign Relations, says “The radicalization of politics on the right and the power of toxic tech are reinforcing and accelerating long-standing gender bias rather than breaking it down.” This is a double blow: the liberatory qualities and euphoria of the early years of the internet are being strangled by the refusal of tech companies to take responsibility or liability for the harms of their technologies-on-steroids. At the same time, governments have failed to mount effective regulation. Related: AI Warfare Goes Unchecked Male populists lead the backlash The targeting of women political leaders by far-right extremists and elected autocratic populists, both online and offline, shouldn’t come as a surprise in the Trump/ Milei/Bolsonaro/Putin/Modi era. Though I confess that I had thought the US was further along in its egalitarian development. However, the rise of Donald Trump shows otherwise. Trump has gleefully fed this backlash with his constant denigration of female politicians and journalists ( here and here ). Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired, forced out, or blocked promotion of a number of high-ranking female military officers, including the chief of Naval Operations, the US military’s representative to NATO and the Coast Guard commandant (he also has dismissed numerous racial minority leaders in the military). These and other right-wing leaders’ constant anti-women jabbering has had the effect of normalizing such attacks: “Boys will be boys, what can you do?” And this is not just a US phenomenon. Around the world, almost half of women legislators have received violent threats and are much more likely to be targeted for their gender than are men, according to the Inter-Parliamentary Union , an international organization of national parliaments. The study found that sexism, harassment and violence against women parliamentarians are very real and pervasive, and exists to different degrees in every country. The IPU report shows a shocking list of harmful and dangerous behaviors directed at female parliamentarians, stretching out along a malicious continuum of abuse: 66% were subject to humiliating sexual or sexist remarks; 42% had humiliating or sexually charged images of themselves spread through digital media; 44% were subjected to threats of death, rape, beatings or abduction; 33% were the victims of harassment in the form of insistent and uninvited behavior or verbal contact that some of the targets found frightening; 26% were subjected to one or more acts of physical violence, and 22% were subjected to one or more acts of sexual violence. That’s shocking: over one fifth of female legislators were subjected to sexual violence. How can a woman legislator focus on doing her job when she is immersed in such a hostile work environment? And when she is hearing constant stories from her female colleagues of their own abuse and mistreatment? The fact that they continue in the face of this persistent male bellicosity and posturing shows an astounding amount of courage. The rising popularity of right-wing political leaders around the world poses a threat to women and democracy, says Robinson from the Council on Foreign Relations. “Populist politicians explicitly attack feminism and gender equality or cloak their regressive stands behind the rhetoric of restoring ‘traditional family values. ’” And they increasingly make gender-based appeals to win votes, including to young men and men of color . Related: Centi-Billionaires Dominating US Media and Politics Threaten Democracy Women’s slow leakage of political power This ongoing demeaning of women by the world’s most powerful male leaders is setting an example that is reversing women’s political gains over the past 20 years. And given the hostile treatment and environment, women are shying away from political office because of this onslaught of violent threats and online abuse. Consequently, women today occupy only 27.5 percent of the world’s legislative seats (about the same as the US , at 28%), even as the number of women leading their countries’ governments has sharply declined. The number of countries (out of 195) with women serving as a head of state or government has fallen from a high of 38 in 2023 to 28 today . High profile female heads-of-state in New Zealand, Finland, Slovakia, Scotland and the Netherlands have resigned or chosen not to run for reelection due to the harassing environment. According to the Center for American Women and Politics , the number of Republican women candidates has declined dramatically , by 28%, since 2022, and the number of women nominees for both Democrats and Republicans has declined. Trump’s regal restoration has been part of a global backlash against women’s political rise. This reactionary rebound has all the hallmarks of a winner-take-all, zero sum game: a perception by many that, for women to win , men must lose . These are very worrisome trends. The battle is on, and its signs have been hiding in plain sight as part of an ongoing assault against the decades-long effort to build a more egalitarian, democratic society. DemocracySOS

articles.title: Death of Journalism
articles.author: Sonali Kolhatkar
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Journalism is experiencing one of its worst crises when it’s needed the most. Overall, news consumption is dropping . And it’s worse among young people , who largely get their news through social media, not news outlets. People under 30, more than any other age group, trust social media sources of news. The problem is that it’s hard to tell if your favorite social media source is a citizen journalist or a paid promoter. In a recent in-depth report , The New York Times revealed that social media platforms are rife with accounts that are paid to promote campaigns parading as personal opinion. Rather than hire well-known influencers with huge followings, politicians and organizations are now hiring huge numbers of accounts with smaller followings. “Functioning more like birdshot than a single bullet,” the Times explained, “these high-volume social media campaigns represent the new vanguard of modern political influence, saturating the internet with a topic until it is all but unavoidable.” Related: Why Economic Justice Requires Racial Justice A perspective that appears popular online may well be the result of this digital “astroturfing.” A decade ago, many Americans blamed the Russian government for insidious meddling in American politics using armies of paid content pushers. Now the same tactic is being deployed by campaigns and nonprofits. This disturbing trend goes hand-in-hand with a shocking decimation of journalism. A June 2026 study found that the number of journalists per capita in the United States fell by more than 80 percent since 2002, and those jobs that remain are increasingly focused on sports and crime rather than public policy, government, or other issues. As out-of-work journalists turn to freelancing, the situation for piecemeal work is equally grim. The National Writers Union recently found that freelance pay remains stagnant even as the cost of living has more than doubled. Desperate to make ends meet, some independent journalists might attempt to garner large enough followings on social media to monetize their work — only to find that they have to play to algorithms designed to lift up rage bait and polarizing content. If our views are shaped by paid content creators, and there are fewer than ever journalists to investigate issues of concern, we face a future where opinions are bought and paid for by those with the deepest pockets. Related: JD Vance Wants to Pay Parents to Stay Home—but With Child Care Money We cannot continue this way. Democracy will die if we have no good answer for funding journalism that is hard-hitting and trustworthy. To address the crisis in journalism, California Governor Gavin Newsom recently signed AB 2222 to strengthen local journalism. Under the law, qualifying news outlets in California will receive $20,000 per journalist , capped at five journalists, plus $15,000 for every additional journalist. This might cover pay raises in a state where $100,000 a year is considered a “low-income” wage — and where the median salary for journalists is under $53,000 . But while the bill’s intentions are laudable, this is too little too late. Thousands of journalists have already left their field. For decades, the federal government diverted a minuscule sliver of the national budget to publicly fund broadcast media through the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. President Donald Trump took a sledgehammer to that modest and very limited source of funding, ending it in July 2025. Related: Is the Growing Backlash Against AI Data Centers Bringing Americans Together? What then, is the answer? If New York City Mayor Mamdani can open city-run grocery stores , can localities do something similar for newsrooms, while preserving the critical editorial independence necessary for good journalism? The answer is “yes.” Media expert Victor Pickard has touted an ambitious and innovative plan for “Public Media Centers” in local communities around the country that are “federally guaranteed but locally owned and controlled.” Study after study proves that journalism fuels and promote a strong democracy. It’s no wonder that authoritarianism is rising at the same time that journalism is dying. If we want to save our democracy, we must save journalism. OtherWords

articles.title: Trump Is Steering
articles.author: Tom Engelhardt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Here’s the truth of it: after all these years, today I don’t know what to write about. I mean, in this ever-stranger world of ours, where even to start? Oh, wait, give me a second and I’ll be right back! I don’t want to miss the latest ads featuring our president , paid for with millions of our tax dollars. It’s obviously important to check them out since, as he told us recently, “I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office. I’m promoting the country.” And who wouldn’t want him to reassure us about the state of this fair land of ours? As he put it in one of those ads, “America will never be a communist country.” Whew! Who among us wasn’t worried about that! Oops, and here I am again! It certainly seems as if my country (though, in truth, it doesn’t exactly feel like mine anymore) is now, to use a classic phrase, distinctly up shit’s creek without a paddle — unless you consider Donald Trump a paddle. If so, there’s little question, of course, that he’s paddling us all to hell and back. And mind you, as I was writing this, the latest polls of voters for the upcoming November elections suggested that I wasn’t alone in thinking such thoughts. A surprising number of Americans, even ones who once voted for him (yes, him!), are now clearly worried that “our” president has put us on that very pathway to hell and, worse yet, the “and back” in that phrase (”to hell and back”) might no longer apply to this all-American world of ours. Buy the Book Even more strikingly, we are evidently on a planet that, in terms of habitability — from the historic (or do I mean ahistorical?) El Niño now developing in the Pacific Ocean to heat, drought, fire , you name it — seems to be going down, down, down, again without a paddle in sight. We are, of course, living in an ever-hotter new world (and not faintly in the ancient all-American sense that the phrase “new world” once had). After all, with record seasonal heat from Europe to North America and distinctly beyond , we humans (not to speak of alligators, elephants, penguins, and turtles) are clearly living on a different planet in a fashion that should seem all too devastating to so many more of us than it evidently yet does. Just consider it good luck that you and I aren’t polar bears living in a distinctly (yes, that word again!) heating Arctic — its sea ice having “shrunk by nearly half a million square kilometers per decade since 1979, equivalent to losing an area the size of Spain every 10 years.” In fact, congratulate yourself if you’re not living in the Swiss Alps, where glaciers have lost nearly one-fifth of their volume over — no, not the past half-century but the last five years! — and between July and September of this year alone, around an additional 2.2 trillion liters of water. Oh, and it’s not just on land either. After all, “more than 90% of emperor penguin colonies could be near extinction by 2100 if sea ice loss persists at its current rate.” Of course, in such a world, it won’t necessarily just be animals potentially going extinct but, perhaps somewhere down the line, we humans, too. (Okay, you’re right! We are indeed “animals.” I certainly didn’t mean to argue with you about that!) Related: Trump, Endless Wars, and the Decline of American Empire Donald Trump Is Doing His Damnedest to Take Us All Down with Him Although all of what I cited above represents the latest news and figures I could find, none of it should really surprise us. After all, it shouldn’t have been hard to learn that such a world was on the way, with one record year of heat succeeding another, and that far worse is clearly still to come. And yet, imagine that, somehow, in 2024, in a world already setting heat records globally, the American people elected a president — for the second time, no less — who refuses even to admit that anything whatsoever climate-related is happening on this planet. (I was tempted to write “of ours,” but it really isn’t anymore, is it?). He, of course, made it all too clear during that election campaign and thereafter that he considered climate change a “ con job .” (Someday, he himself will undoubtedly be known as the con-job president.) We’re talking about an 80-year-old guy who’s clearly starting to lose it (and given that I’m referring to Donald J. Trump, who even knows quite what that “it” means). In the process, he’s quite literally doing his — yes, what an appropriate world under the circumstances! — damnedest to take us all down with him. Worse yet, in the midst of what should be the greatest crisis in human history, we — in particular Donald Trump (Iran), Vladimir Putin (Ukraine), and Benjamin Netanyahu (Gaza and Southern Lebanon, not to speak of Iran, too), and of course local leaders from Myanmar to Sudan to Somalia (again with a helping hand from Donald Trump) — seem to be doing our damnedest to make things so much worse, since war pours fossil fuels into the atmosphere in a stunning fashion. And keep in mind that Vladimir Putin, the climate-change-averse leader of Russia, has now begun threatening to turn to that other method of global destruction humanity possesses for the first time since my country dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945 to end World War II. I’m thinking about nuclear weapons, of course, to salvage (or do I mean savage?) his war in Ukraine. (Oh, and he seems to be planning, however indirectly , to harm Ukraine’s nuclear power plants as well.) Honestly, you couldn’t make most of this up, could you? And who even knows what I’ve left out. As for the future, however uninventive we may be when it comes to lending this planet a hand, give us full credit, since we continue to be all too inventive when it comes to making war on each other and increasingly on the planet itself. Related: Trump Is Fighting the Future—and China Is Winning In early October, as I was writing this, the weather in my town, New York City, breached 80 degrees, and they’re predicting warmer-than-usual weather all fall here. (What a shock!) Of course, no one should be faintly surprised by that or any other news like it. Across the planet, an increasing heat hell seems to be causing violent avalanches in the Himalayas and wiping out glaciers in the Alps. In fact, you name it and it’s probably already happening on this ever more disturbed planet of ours. And worse yet, count on this: unless we act with reasonable focus and speed, everything I’ve mentioned is likely to grow so much worse in the years to come. Yes, in terms of green energy, we increasingly have the means to put a brake on all of this. But perhaps it tells you everything you need to know that China, the greatest producer of green energy (and the equipment to make it) on this planet right now, also remains the greatest user of fossil fuels. And don’t even get me started on that giant user of fossil fuels , AI! All in all, tell me that we’re not indeed up shit’s creek without a paddle. Tom's Substack

articles.title: Climate Policies Can Bring Relief on Affordability and Beyond
articles.author: Rithika Ramamurthy
articles.content: As the US midterm elections approach, one word keeps coming up in campaign promises and headlines: “ affordability .” That working people in the United States are struggling to afford basic necessities is a problem that many are willing to acknowledge, but there is very little agreement on what should be done to tackle a core driver of the affordability crisis: climate change. The climate crisis is already making life more expensive . Electricity rates skyrocketed in 2025 due to historic heat waves; home insurance rates are rising as disasters and extreme weather patterns increase; transportation costs have become one of the biggest sources of financial burden because of the volatile price of fossil fuels. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has withdrawn from global climate commitments, leaped into costly oil wars abroad, backed the deeply unpopular expansion of AI build-out across the country, and continuously decried renewable energy as a “green new scam.” Failing to act on climate change while entrenching fossil fuel dependency deepens the affordability crisis, inflating the cost of living for working people as the economy buckles under the weight of various forms of environmental instability. And it also threatens the planet in both the environmental and political senses. Ignoring the climate crisis is not only an economically unsound tactic; it is also a politically unpopular one. Climate and Community Institute’s polling with Data for Progress earlier this year showed that people have connected the dots between their strained budgets and climate change: 80 percent said that extreme weather phenomena impacted their cost of living, and 55 percent said that they wanted elected officials to address climate change and the cost of living through coordinated policies. Political pundits pushing “ climate hushing ” — leaving climate out of kitchen-table politics — present a false choice between economic and climate policy and are ignoring what people need. One clear takeaway from the implementation of the Inflation Reduction Act and the legacy of the Joe Biden presidency is that durable climate policy must address the cost-of-living crisis but also implement transformative changes that people can feel in their everyday lives. Climate change is making everything from home insurance to groceries more expensive , but it is also making life more difficult and dangerous . We urgently need an ambitious agenda that connects the dots and offers rapid change to working people’s material conditions across the economy. Immediate relief policies can take on the climate and economic crises at once, beginning with lowering costs inflated by climate change and alleviating other economic issues. A new series of briefs by the Climate and Community Institute demonstrates how to deliver that relief across the spectrum of everyday life in the areas where people are intensely feeling the effects of the climate crisis. These policies do not treat climate as an add-on or afterthought to piecemeal affordability measures. They alleviate pain points where people need help, from their health to their cooling costs, by moving federal dollars through the budget reconciliation process. In this approach, “relief” is not just about putting money back in people’s pockets. It requires a whole-economy approach that cuts costs, protects people, and allows them to thrive — all of which require dealing with environmental instability. Actually tackling climate change by decarbonizing the economy will be a long process, but people need relief in the here and now. Putting forward bold policies that show that the government can deliver things quickly and to meet needs is a necessary part of any popular and successful political agenda that wants to win a greener, fairer future. Cutting Costs and Protecting People Because climate change is making life more expensive, financial burden is one of the primary ways that people feel the impacts of the climate crisis in their daily lives. Climate policies can provide immediate relief by focusing on cutting costs. Take electricity, for example, a popular focus in affordability conversations. Electricity costs have exploded in recent years because of the massive data center build-out, extreme weather, and foreign wars increasing already-volatile fossil fuel prices. As residential electricity rates have risen, more and more people have fallen into utility debt. One in six households are behind on their power bills. Meanwhile, utilities are working hand in glove with data center developers and tech companies, creating huge bill increases for everyday people. The federal government can create an Electricity Debt Cancellation Program , which would provide $20 billion in forgivable loans to utility companies conditioned on eliminating all residential ratepayer debt, reconnecting users, and submitting a concrete affordability plan that tackles the root causes of increased electricity prices, like the climate crisis and data center explosion. This would save people in the United States millions in utility bills and also show them that the federal government can and should intervene more explicitly in managing utilities to keep rates affordable and make electricity green and reliable during extreme weather events. Beyond financial instability, climate policy can also protect people from the threats to their survival exacerbated by the climate crisis. Extreme heat, hurricanes, wildfires, and severe storms are not just increasing costs for communities already facing a broader affordability crisis but damaging homes and infrastructure while endangering and displacing people. Federal responses to disaster is one salient part of this picture: instead of building out the public institutions that deliver security, like the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the Trump administration has been gutting the already under-resourced agency in order to divert funds for staffing and capacity to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), even as FEMA was facing increased demands for emergency disaster response. The consequences are twofold: not only are ICE’s operations violating people’s rights, but FEMA is forced to help carry out deportations and immigration enforcement rather than disaster relief. Congress can alleviate these harms by reducing the ICE budget and redirecting resources to FEMA to better fund disaster response as the climate crisis intensifies. Redirecting federal investment from militarized police to disaster response would not only keep people safe from ICE’s intensely unpopular and violent enforcement tactics, but it would allow Department of Homeland Security funding to go to much-needed scaling up of the public institution responsible for protecting people facing hurricanes, wildfires, extreme heat, and flooding. As of June 2026, more than $100 billion was provided to ICE through budget reconciliation that has gone unused. Moving that money to be used by FEMA would demonstrate that safety can be built through state capacity and preparedness rather than coercive enforcement. A Right to Thrive Beyond bringing down the knock-on financial costs from the climate crisis and mitigating direct harm, immediate relief should also support the right to thrive in the fullest sense. Most working people are not only struggling to pay for electricity bills and home insurance premiums, they are suffering from lower quality of life overall. People are working more, making less, and lonelier than ever — and the climate crisis is making this worse. One way to fix this is through policies that work to adapt communities. The federal government can invest just $10 billion in public parks that would provide outdoor space for community interaction, increase flood absorbency, and offer heat relief in the summer months. Access to public works is not just important for people’s sense of quality of life; it can provide much-needed green infrastructure as cities and towns adapt to a changing climate. As the United States faces a dire cost-of-living crisis, affordability should be an anchoring priority to provide immediate relief to working people. Climate policy should be central to any agenda that provides this economic relief, and it can also go beyond cutting costs here and there to bringing immediate relief across the spectrum of everyday life. By acting quickly to move federal investments, Congress can show that government can accomplish the first steps of a capacious agenda that brings relief to millions of people who need it. articles.title: Historian Eric Hobsbawm Was a “Communist Polymath”
articles.author: Emile Chabal
articles.content: Eric Hobsbawm’s life began just as the “long nineteenth century” was drawing to a close. Born in Alexandria, Egypt, and formed as a youth in Red Vienna and Weimar-era Berlin, he came to intellectual maturity in interwar Cambridge and postwar London. His Ages tetralogy firmly established him on course syllabi and on the bookshelves of what he called, in The Age of Revolution , “the intelligent and educated citizen, who is not merely curious about the past, but wishes to understand how and why the world has come to be what it is today and whither it is going.” And he was, paradoxically for someone who rose to such popular heights, a proud communist who, for better or worse depending on whom you ask, bound himself to a particular vision of a better future as he bore witness to an epoch he dubbed the “age of extremes.” Yet despite being, as his biographer Emile Chabal puts it, a “communist polymath, with a remarkable reach over the theoretical and empirical landscape of modern history,” Hobsbawm, unlike many of his continental counterparts, “rarely features in the canon of left-wing or Marxist thought.” Why that is so is one of the questions animating Chabal’s fascinating and wide-ranging new intellectual history, The Age of Hobsbawm . Chabal is a professor of contemporary history at the University of Edinburgh, and the book’s publication brought him up to St Andrews, Scotland, for an author event at our local independent bookstore . It is a testament to Hobsbawm’s enduring appeal that even now, in a town dominated by golf enthusiasts and posh students, a crowd of unreconstructed Marxists from the 1970s, left-wing autodidacts, and curious graduate students turned up for a spirited discussion of the theory and politics of the twentieth-century left and their prospects today. What follows is an extension of our conversation that evening and an introduction to Hobsbawm’s world and legacy. Michael Schapira You mention in the preface that you initially had designs on “writing a history of postwar French Marxism, which would capture some of the richness and complexity of radical politics in France.” But you soon realized you could “achieve the same goals by looking closely at Hobsbawm.” Hobsbawm had strong connections to French intellectual life and Eurocommunism more generally, but both he and British Marxism have a very different flavor than their French variants. In what sense did Hobsbawm satisfy your initial aspirations, and how did shifting the focus to him open new avenues to explore radical postwar politics? Emile Chabal When I started working on Hobsbawm in late 2012, I was a freshly minted postdoc. I’d spent the previous five years working on contemporary French history and politics, so it was perhaps inevitable that French concepts like the “intellectual” and the Sartrean idea of engagement [in English, “commitment”] loomed so large in my mind. You are right though: postwar British Marxism has a very different flavor from its French (or continental) counterpart. It was less abstract, less ideological, and less overtly philosophical. What is interesting about Hobsbawm is that he straddled the British and continental European intellectual traditions much more than his other British Marxist contemporaries. As a student in the late 1930s, he was profoundly shaped by the peculiar environment of Cambridge, but he also saw himself as an integral part of a global communist movement with its base in Paris. After World War II, when he wanted to make his name as a historian, he continued to move between Britain and continental Europe in an effort to find useful interlocutors and mentors. As I learned more about Hobsbawm’s incessant back-and-forth between the UK and Europe, I was grateful for having been a scholar of France in my younger days; it gave me a unique perspective on his intellectual formation and identity. And it also helped me bridge the often rather sterile divide between the intellectual histories of radical politics in the English-speaking world and continental Europe. Michael Schapira Toward the end of his life, Hobsbawm returned to his formative years in Vienna and Weimar Berlin, framing his experience as that of a generational cohort whose worldview was fading. However, he also developed habits of mind and manner that clearly reflected his years at Cambridge and became recognizably British in so many aspects of his writing and work. This reminded me of Owen Hatherley’s wonderful profile of Central European émigrés who arrived in Britain around the same time as Hobsbawm and were, in the words of Walter Gropius, shocked by the “sentiment-laden inartistic world” that greeted them. This may be unfairly reductive, but did Hobsbawm meaningfully retain this “alienation effect,” as Hatherley puts it, or did aspects of his biography and personality make him especially suited to British cultural and political life? Emile Chabal I think it’s important to emphasize that Hobsbawm was not a Central European émigré or refugee. He followed a similar trajectory (in his case, from Vienna to Berlin to London in the mid-1930s), and he certainly felt that London in 1933 was desperately boring compared to Berlin. But he was a British national and a native English speaker. When he arrived in London, he had, on paper, come “home,” even if he had never lived in the UK. He was therefore an outsider, not a foreigner. It would be more accurate, then, to see the young Hobsbawm engaged in a very rapid process of acculturation and assimilation after his arrival in London — and, since he was only a teenager, he discovered that the school system was a very good way of becoming British. Inevitably, this meant that some of his most obviously British qualities — his intellectual agility, his commitment to concision, his facility with self-deprecating rhetoric and debate — were forged during his final years of high school in London and as a student at Cambridge. These intellectual traits were easily recognizable for the rest of his life. In other ways, however, he was not very British at all. It is noteworthy, for instance, how little class discomfort he appears to have felt. Most British left-wing intellectuals of his generation — whether communist or not — were resentful, if not angry, about the straitjacket of the British class system, but Hobsbawm’s class coordinates lay elsewhere, in the bourgeois universe of Central Europe. Crucially, he missed the vital period between late childhood and early teenage years when the British class system is most aggressively inculcated through schooling and wider society. By the time he arrived, he could simply transcend class prejudices by being extremely good at school (and, later, at university). This made him remarkably tolerant of manifestations of class prejudice in Britain’s higher educational system. If he disliked High Table at Cambridge, it was because he found the people boring, not because it was an expression of class inequality! Michael Schapira Hobsbawm is unusual in his commitment to communism — especially of a Leninist, party-led variant. Whereas so many took 1956 as an off-ramp from the cause completely or charted a new path (including those who would found influential journals like New Left Review ), Hobsbawm stayed the course to the best of his abilities. This is most clearly on display in his 1994 BBC interview with Michael Ignatieff, where he defends what Ignatieff considers an indefensible position: supporting the aspirations of communism in the wake of the events of the twentieth century. Do you think this helps explain why he never really found a home in the canon of Marxist thought? And how does it square with his elevation to the status of a celebrity intellectual and best-selling author? Emile Chabal Following on from the previous question, one could argue that Hobsbawm’s commitment to communism was another decidedly un-British character trait of his. Rather than adopt a pragmatic position toward the future of the Left by moving away from the Communist Party after 1956, he maintained his attachment to a political idea, which is exactly the kind of “dogmatism” that many in Britain saw (and still see) as a pathology of continental European politics. Hence, I think, why many of his interviews in the 1990s — including the famous one with Ignatieff — were so awkward. He and Ignatieff were talking past each other: Hobsbawm was trying to explain his deep commitment to an ideal, a future utopia, something that transcended him, whereas Ignatieff was insisting he make a moralistic judgment. It’s interesting to reflect on how Hobsbawm’s communism might have affected the reception of his work and his mass-market success. I don’t actually believe that his communism is the reason for his relative neglect in the Marxist “canon.” I think this has much more to do with the fact that he always presented himself as a “historian,” not as a “theorist.” In the book, I try to make the case that Hobsbawm was quite a serious thinker and that he had a strong theoretical grounding, but some might disagree with me, simply because he worked so hard to downplay his theoretical credentials. What is unquestionably true is that he was a mass-market publishing sensation, and this may well have had to do with his communism. Paradoxically, though, it’s probably not because people saw his writings as dogmatically communist — a novice reader of Age of Extremes might not even realize he was a Marxist! — but because his communist framing of history provided a powerful basis for his work. Many people have been attracted to Hobsbawm’s writings because they feel as if history is in motion in his texts; this derives, in large part, from his underlying philosophy of history. Michael Schapira You have extensive chapters devoted to Hobsbawm’s work as a critic (e.g., of jazz, on which he wrote a regular column) and his travels around the world. These inclusions expanded the project tremendously, including interviews with figures from around the world but also opening up a whole new archive of writings that many might not take to be central to his work. When did these become an important part of your project? Emile Chabal Yes, I am proud of these chapters in the book! In both my exploration of him as a cultural critic and in the section devoted to his travels, I wanted to widen the frame of intellectual history to take in different kinds of writing. It was particularly important to me to show that Hobsbawm was as much a journalist as he was an academic — and that the two identities were mutually reinforcing. Given that he was a lifelong academic and very clearly a professional historian, it might seem odd to put his journalistic and scholarly writings on the same level, but all you have to do is look at his bibliography: he published hundreds and hundreds of journalistic op-eds, essays, and reviews. They were a huge part of his published corpus. In the pages of the New Statesman , Rinascita , or the Times Literary Supplement , you can see him commenting on current affairs and working out new ideas (about the role of culture in society, for example). I expect it was the work I did on the complete Eric Hobsbawm online bibliography in 2019–2020 that really brought home to me the importance of these supposedly ephemeral writings. Michael Schapira As part of the chapters on his travels, you have descriptions of Hobsbawm’s extensive use of interviews and conversations, sometimes in methodologically questionable ways. In the back of your book, there is a long list of interviews you conducted with historians, activists, politicians, and others over several years and in various locales. What inspired you to extend beyond traditional archival research and embark on this ambitious interview project? Emile Chabal I always wanted the book to be global so that it would reflect the global character of its subject. But, as Hobsbawm himself knew very well, one’s global ambitions are limited by the hard cash that is available. And so it was for me: it was only when I was awarded a major fellowship grant in 2017 that I was able to undertake interviews in India, Brazil, Peru, Chile, Argentina, Mexico, the United States, France, Germany, and the UK. These were primarily with Hobsbawm’s friends, students, colleagues, and those influenced by him, and they were tremendously useful to me as I was trying to frame Hobsbawm’s life within a global context. But they also did something more: they helped me understand how Hobsbawm approached foreign countries. He and I did similar things. We both arrived in a new city with an address book and sought out interesting people with whom to talk. In this way, the time I spent interviewing members of the twenty-first-century left intelligentsia gave me a unique insight into how Hobsbawm did more or less the same thing half a century before. Michael Schapira In our talk at Topping & Company Bookshop in St Andrews, an audience member reminisced about the Marxist grandees who made up his curriculum at Warwick in the 1970s. And of them, Hobsbawm has had the most enduring power. Bernie Sanders and Jeremy Corbyn, arguably responsible for the biggest injection of energy into left-wing electoral politics in recent times, were also relics of a less fashionable era of leftist thought, closer to Hobsbawm. Why do you think this is? Does it have something to do with another topic you discuss in the book, namely the Left’s history of dealing with disappointment and defeat? Emile Chabal There’s no question that being on the Left — whatever we take that to mean — involves accepting and rationalizing defeat. Enzo Traverso has written very eloquently about the “left-wing melancholia” that has been part of the story of the Left since the defeat of the Paris Commune in 1871. Hobsbawm embodied this tradition: he understood the history of the Left to be one of adversity. This is part of the reason why he did not take the myriad “failures” of the Left during his lifetime — from the [Treaty of Non-Aggression between Germany and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics] of 1939 through to the crushing defeats meted out to the British Labour Party in the 1980s — as a sign that he should jump ship. Having said that, I agree with Traverso when he says that the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 was a more fundamental and unsettling kind of defeat than anything that had happened before. You can see this even in Hobsbawm’s private correspondence in the early 1990s, where he was forced to reckon with the total failure of his lifetime of political commitment. And yet he came out fighting: in public, at least, he defended communism, and he refused to recant his beliefs. I think this sort of steadfast commitment to a political ideal is something that is very difficult to understand for left-wing activists born into the post–Cold War world. They look at Hobsbawm — or Sanders or Corbyn — and see a certainty about the future that they don’t have. Some admire this certainty and want it to be the foundation of a renewed left, but it’s also important to recognize that it was the product of a very particular set of mid-twentieth-century historical circumstances, none of which exist today. Michael Schapira Perhaps we can conclude by returning to the present. By his own admission, Hobsbawm was not someone whom you’d find shoulder to shoulder with factory workers or miners on the front lines of class struggle. But one area where he was directly active was in the university, an institution that nurtured and formed the basis of his scholarly output. At the moment, you are several weeks into a strike at the University of Edinburgh as conditions across the “higher education sector” continue to deteriorate across Great Britain and elsewhere. How did working on this project over the past decade inform your understanding of continuities and changes in the status and nature of the university in the past seventy years? Emile Chabal Hobsbawm entered the university system as a student at Cambridge in 1936, and he remained in it until the end of his post-retirement visiting professorship at the New School in New York in the mid-1990s. He never took extended sabbaticals beyond the standard allowance, and he continued teaching in some way or another throughout his career. He was as fully institutionalized as was possible within the higher educational structures of the time. The fact that he was able to be productive and successful while depending on his university for financial support and logistical infrastructure should give those of us who are in a similar situation today some reassurance. Hobsbawm too got tired of marking essays, chasing collaborators, and doing university paperwork! And yet something feels different about the twenty-first century. This could be because universities in Western Europe and North America are now contracting, whereas they were expanding in the 1950s, ’60s, and ’70s. This could also be because wage deflation has made it increasingly difficult to aspire to a comfortable middle-class life on a university salary. To me, though, the real difference lies in the dramatically enhanced role of public-sector institutions — like universities — in postwar Europe, a point Hobsbawm himself discussed in the late 1970s in his famous lecture “The Forward March of Labour Halted?” When Hobsbawm first became a professional academic in the late 1940s, universities were small and elite institutions, but their rapid growth made them — especially in Europe — essential components of local and regional economies. Today they are every bit as important as factories were in the early twentieth century, and the closure or bankruptcy of a university risks the same catastrophic effects that many European countries experienced during deindustrialization in the 1970s and ’80s. That is why today’s fight to defend higher education feels existential in a way that it did not for Hobsbawm and his generation. articles.title: How Bernie’s Campaigns Reorganized the Organized Left
articles.author: Hadas Thier
articles.content: Ten years ago, while socialist Bernie Sanders was making his historic run for the Democratic presidential nomination that drew millions of supporters and promised a “political revolution” to live long past his campaign, I was part of a small revolutionary organization that pooh-poohed him as a faux renegade. The socialist left at the time had been largely marginal to the American political landscape. This was not only because so few socialists sat in political offices. Organized socialists were unable to insert our ideas, strategies, or demands beyond small meetings and study groups, only occasionally influencing national discourse by being part of movements that showed themselves on the street in mass numbers. But movements naturally ebb and flow, and in their absence, much of the Left would retreat back into itself time and again. In 2016, Bernie Sanders showed that socialists could be relevant to mainstream discourse, could move the needle on major policy issues, and could do so on the basis of a class politics that resonates widely and deeply around the country. Though he didn’t win that primary nor the following one in 2020, Bernie’s runs transformed the mainstream political landscape and, along with it, the organized left. The section of the Left that threw itself in with Bernie’s campaigns — most significantly, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) — grew exponentially in both numbers and influence and developed a deep well of experience and savvy. The section of the Left that scorned his campaigns in favor of independence from the Democratic Party and time-honored revolutionary principles stagnated or fell apart, leaving DSA and electoral projects at the forefront of an ascendant movement. The Left was thus reorganized to take the lead from Bernie’s “political revolution,” where electoralism was one important piece of a broad strategy to contend for power and build a mass politics. Ten years on, that political revolution continues to grow, while the approach of smaller socialist sects that had characterized so much of the pre-2016 left has receded into the background. We need not return to the path of permanent outsiders ever again. With DSA a powerful political force in the country and democratic socialist elected officials making concrete strides forward for working people, the intraleft debates that surfaced in 2016 are largely settled. They offer important lessons about the pitfalls of a sectarian approach that places organizational identity above building the biggest and most powerful left and holds rigidly onto traditional principles above shifting political realities. 2016 Was a Turning Point 2016 was an odd time for the radical left. For those of us standing outside of the most transformational development within the American political landscape to have taken place in many years, having to explain that Bernie wasn’t a true socialist to scores of newly energized and activated young people made us feel like killjoys, no matter how we tried to spin it. The group that I was a member of, the International Socialist Organization (ISO), insisted that we could relate to the movement around Bernie without supporting its candidate, by showing up to rallies with our newspaper and by engaging in organizing work around demands like Medicare for All. The main thrust of our argument served as a wet blanket. The radical left quibbled with some of Bernie’s positions, but his cardinal sin was collaboration with the Democratic Party and the fact that, despite decades of holding political office as an independent, he was running for president within the Democratic primary. The reasoning behind the argument isn’t entirely wrong: the Democratic Party is a party controlled by big business. Ruling elites have traded political power among themselves through the Democratic and Republican parties for over 150 years. The entrenchment of the two-party system in the United States is unique in comparison to other capitalist democracies. Because of antidemocratic and restrictive barriers to entry into the electoral arena, independent parties of the working class, poor farmers, and the oppressed have struggled heroically — and largely failed — to assert themselves or break the stranglehold of the two parties. In that context, Bernie Sanders and others who have followed in his footsteps since have opted to run for political office utilizing the Democratic Party and its open primary elections. Despite the conservative leadership of the party, Sanders wagered, socialist politics could appeal to the base of the party and create a movement from within. Sanders understood it was a serious problem that workers didn’t have their own party and were largely stuck with the Democrats, but also that the structural limitations of American politics made a break with them impossible in the short term. So he developed a strategy of running for president within the Democratic Party and engaging mass numbers of Americans while remaining independent of and often explicitly hostile to the party’s elites. Many on the already existing radical left weren’t buying it. Bernie was just another “sheepdog,” according to Bruce Dixon of Black Agenda Report , “charged with herding activists and voters back into the Democratic fold who might otherwise drift leftward and outside of the Democratic Party.” Howie Hawkins, a Green Party leader who himself had run for various offices on the Green Party line, argued at the time: “Sanders is violating the first principle of socialist politics: class independence.” Bernie’s positions on the issues, he explained, are “secondary to the question of whether his politics are helping the working class act for itself or subsume itself under the big business interests in charge of the Democratic Party.” According to this line of argument, the party leadership actually benefits from such campaigns, because the campaigns reengage otherwise disaffected voters. The “well-trodden path” worn by Dennis Kucinich was the prime example. Running in the Democratic primaries for president twice, in 2004 and 2008, on a platform opposing war in Iraq and in support of single-payer health care, he garnered less than 4 percent of votes, eventually throwing his support behind John Kerry and then Barack Obama. The radical left assumed the same fate for Bernie Sanders in 2016. “The Democratic establishment can breathe a collective sigh of relief,” argued one Socialist Worker article. “It doesn’t, in fact, fear liberal Democrats like Kucinich or Sanders, but third-party challenges like [Ralph] Nader’s that have the prospect of breaking their stranglehold on votes from workers and the oppressed, as several local and statewide campaigns have shown over the last few years.” From there flowed a familiar refrain of arguments: No sustained movement would come of it. The Democrats have always functioned as the “graveyard of social movements.” Radicals attempting to change the Democratic Party would only end up changed themselves, ostensibly into toothless reformists. And the old favorite, quoting historian Howard Zinn: “What matters most is not who is sitting in the White House, but ‘who is sitting in’ — and who is marching outside the White House, pushing for change.” The only revolutionary socialist organization to endorse Sanders was Socialist Alternative. It took the awkward tack of endorsing Bernie while urging him to run as an independent in the general election, in the likely event that he lost the primary (although he had made it clear, in no uncertain terms, that he would not do so). It tried to distinguish its politics from the larger DSA, which was much more integrated into Bernie’s campaign. Meanwhile, the American Stalinist organization the Party for Socialism and Liberation (PSL) ran its own candidate for president but more enthusiastically greeted the Bernie movement as a positive step for the socialist left, frowning upon the strategy of other socialists for calling out Bernie as “not a real socialist.” By 2020, it would argue for critical support of Sanders’s campaign. Of course, what actually happened in 2016 didn’t follow the expected script. Entering the campaign with no name recognition and polling just 3 percent at the start, Sanders went on to win twenty-three primaries and caucuses and about 46 percent of pledged delegates at the Democratic National Convention. Leaked emails among Democratic National Committee members (who, as it turned out, were much more afraid of Sanders than they ever were of third-party challengers like Nader) exposed behind-the-scenes work in the committee to help Hillary Clinton secure the nomination. Bernie did endorse and campaign for Clinton in the general election, as promised. But that didn’t stop millions of his supporters from learning a bitter lesson about the party’s establishment. The word “socialist” went from a slur to a point of pride. The “political revolution” that Sanders promised came to be through a growing number of democratic socialist campaigns, from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s upset victory over ten-term incumbent Joe Crowley in 2018 through to Zohran Mamdani’s New York City mayoralty today. But while the Left as a whole was buoyed by Bernie’s 2016 run, some radical socialist organizations floundered. DSA grew exponentially by the tens of thousands, and groups like the ISO shrank. Three years later, when it came time to decide how to relate to the 2020 election, most of the revolutionary left opted to just run it back. What could arguably have been considered an understandable mistake in 2016 was by 2019 a different ballgame. Sanders had proven that it was possible to make a serious run; that millions would be radicalized rather than sheepdogged; that tens of thousands would become politically activated in a more long-term way, whether through joining an organization like DSA or by taking inspiration to organize their own workplace . But despite the fact that reality did not play out in the way that the theory had said that it would, the revolutionary left doubled down. Unwilling to adapt the theory to fit new realities or even to acknowledge obvious truths standing right in front of it, the revolutionary left made clear that opposition to the Democratic Party was its core political identity. That identity was hard to part with, and it precluded a serious political and strategic discussion of how to go about rebuilding the Left in a country where the undemocratic two-party system has a stranglehold over electoral politics. So much so that a remotely viable third-party challenge, on a national level, has not happened in a very long time. Lessons for Today As the Left reorganized, three critical lessons emerged. First, theory, even that which has been elevated to first principles, is good only insofar as it explains the world around us. If we can’t question our a priori assumptions when they no longer fit reality, then we have become pure propagandists. Second, if those principles become your identity and the organization holding that identity becomes more important than the health of a broad, effective left, then you have become a sect rather than a serious political project. In the ISO, which I was still a member of in 2019, a small group of us attempted to shift the organization’s electoral strategy to allow for endorsing Bernie Sanders and other socialist candidates running on the Democratic Party ballot line and were met with dismay from the majority of the organization. One document written against our proposal understandably argued that willingness to work within Democratic Party campaigns “logically spells the end of the ISO as a distinct organization on the left.” Pointing out that without a hard abstention from the Democratic Party, the ISO’s politics would be “virtually indistinguishable from the left-wing socialist currents inside DSA,” the document asked: “Why would someone eschew joining a vibrant and growing organization of 40,000 socialists — which includes a growing faction that accords with their politics completely — in favor of joining a political facsimile which is not only outside of DSA but boasts a membership that is a mere 3% of the size of DSA?” The assumption that carried the argument was that the ISO’s brand, identity, and survival as an organization were paramount. This was not because members of the ISO, or any other radical socialist organization, were particularly inclined toward sectarianism. But the many years and decades of operating in isolation, which were imposed by a historically weak Left and labor movement, had left their mark. Detached from working-class movements, the Left developed deeply harmful habits and a mindset that assumes that your organization’s preservation is critical above all else. Lastly, while revolutionary socialists weren’t wrong in their assessment that it’s a huge problem that the Left doesn’t have its own party, they were wrong in their prescription for how we get there and wrong in their assumption that a third party is on the agenda at this moment. Some pointed to polls showing widespread support for a third party. In fact, at least 40 percent of Americans have told Gallup a third party is needed every time it has asked the question since 2003, and majorities have said so in every poll since 2013. But the idea of a third party is very different from actually voting for a third party that has no chance of winning in a system stacked against it. Thus in 2016, while millions donated to, and over 13 million voted for, Bernie Sanders, Green Party candidate Jill Stein received 1.5 million votes, just over 1 percent of the total. The high points of third-party electoralism included Ralph Nader’s 2000 run, which garnered less than 3 percent of the vote and in which Nader was excluded from ever appearing at a presidential debate. As a socialist, I helped lead a Nader 2000 committee at the time, and the experience showed a huge potential for organizing vibrant electoral campaigns. But Nader’s relegation to “spoiler” status by our undemocratic electoral system made it impossible to make substantive headway on Election Day. Worse, the backlash against Nader’s campaign once George W. Bush won (arguably stole) the election by a slim margin only further set back the left electoral project. Even Eugene Debs, the American socialist movement’s greatest popularizer, won 6 percent of the vote in 1912. The Populist Party made its most impressive national gain in the 1892 presidential election with just over 8 percent of the popular vote. Today, with democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani the mayor in New York City, making good on promises to freeze rent and provide universal childcare, the popularity of socialist ideals is soaring, with a majority of young people, women, and people of color favoring socialism over capitalism. Meanwhile, a recent CNN poll showed the Democratic Party’s favorability ratings at a low of 30 percent, while Mamdani, Ocasio-Cortez, and Bernie Sanders top most lists of politicians by popularity. It seems that their campaigns, rather than rehabilitating the Democratic Party, have accentuated the fissures within it. Democratic socialist politicians, no matter their popularity, haven’t been immune to criticism either — a point brought home when Sanders’s slowness to call out Israeli genocide in Gaza earned him scorn from his own supporters. Ten years after Bernie’s first presidential run, his political revolution is still in its early stages. Organizing an independent left pole within the Democratic Party has already scored significant victories, strengthened insurgent left organizing, and popularized the ideals of socialism to millions of people. The Left has grown quickly over the past decade. Despite largely settling the question of whether we can work within the Democratic Party, which was so anathema to many radicals before 2016, we must still grapple with questions of how to do so effectively while avoiding the pitfalls that so many previous American leftists have fallen into in engaging with the party. Winning mass-based electoral campaigns against the Democratic establishment is the first hurdle. But navigating the complexities and contradictions of socialist governance in a capitalist state is a harder hurdle to clear. If we can absorb the lessons that Bernie first started teaching us a decade ago — shedding permanent outsider status and purity politics in favor of broad-based organizing, avoiding the pitfalls of sectarianism in favor of building a powerful left, and discarding rigid theoretical commitments in favor of tactical flexibility rooted in firmly held political principles — who knows where the Left will be another decade from now?
