articles.title: Proles: A Story of Post-Sixties’ Salting Among the “Salt of The Earth”
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: In the early 1970s, when many student activists were migrating from campus to industrial jobs to promote working class radicalization, no labor film was more influential than Salt of the Earth. This pioneering docudrama was made two decades earlier by a producer, writer, director, and several actors who were unemployable in Hollywood, due to McCarthy era-blacklisting. This left-wing creative team recruited a cast of workers and their families from the International Union of Mine, Mill, and Smelter Workers (IUMMSW) to play themselves in a fictional account of a long strike at the Empire Zinc Company in Grant County, New Mexico. Local 890 members knew something about red-baiting too. Shortly before their 1951 fight for better conditions and an end to wage disparities between Anglo and Chicano workers, Mine, Mill was expelled from the Congress of Industrial Organizations (CIO), along with the left-led United Electrical Workers (UE) and west coast longshore union, the ILWU. In In real life, and later on screen, the key to the success of this mining community struggle was the militant participation of strikers’ wives, mothers, daughters and sisters after their own mass picketing is enjoined by a local judge. In Salt of the Earth, this picket-line replacement strategy, which challenged and changed traditional gender roles in a socially conservative company town, is heatedly debated by film’s two lead characters. Blacklisted and Deported Playing the role of Ramon Quintera, Juan Chacon, an actual IUMMSW local president, initially objects to the strike activism of his fictional wife Esperanza, played by Mexican actress Rosaura Revueltas (who was deported for making the film). Other members of an entirely male and largely Latino workforce are similarly conflicted about the emergence of a vocal and empowered women’s auxiliary. When Esperanza and her fellow female pickets are arrested, she takes her small baby behind bars with her. The resulting boisterous jail house protest—which prefigures southern civil rights and peace movement tactics in the 1960s--forces the sheriff to release them all. The miners’ subsequent defense of the Quintera family--when the company tries to evict them--becomes a turning point in the long strike which ends in a contract settlement. Berkeley journalist and now first-time novelist Barry Bergman was among the many young radicals much inspired by this now iconic depiction of Mexican-American labor struggle. Before Bergman relocated to California and began a long career as a newspaper reporter, magazine writer/editor, and communications specialist for UC Berkeley and numerous non-profits, he worked for several years in a copper smelter near Tucson. That experience as a rank-and-file member of the United Steel Workers (USW)--which gobbled up the IUMMSW, after years of raiding it--led to his writing Proles . (Serving House Books). Bergman’s novel is a funny, moving, and historically accurate account of workplace “colonizing”—or “salting” as it’s called today-- told from the point of view of the author’s fictional alter-ego. Via a college course entitled “Celluloid and Social Change,” Simon Bussbaum learns about a film called City of Emeralds. He is captivated by its depiction of “dirt-poor Chicano miners in the Southwest” and their humble but charismatic leader, Naldo Galvin. Art Imitates Life Simon does further research and discovers that Galvin—like the real-life Juan Chacon in the 1970s—has become a dissident in the Steel Workers. The former strike organizer—and Salt of the Earth co-star-- is now rallying his co-workers against “a class collaborationist union which muscled its way into zinc and copper mines in the Sun Belt” by marketing itself as a labor-management partner, rather than a class struggle foe. The bookish film buff from Queens (the author’s hometown as well) leaves anti-war politics behind for a very different blue-collar life in open shop Arizona. Arriving for his first shift at Cobra Copper Company (aka “ThreeCo”) near Turcson, Simon walks into a scene lifted from the film that inspired his turn toward the working class. “Outside the giant garage doors that opened out from the smelter’s shell, hundreds of men clustered in small groups, coveralls gone or dangling at their waist. Some were standing, others lying on bare ground or using their hardhats for seats. A handful were shirtless, glistening in the sun. It might have been a disorderly line at the Fillmore East, save for the work clothes and industrial boots.” A new co-worker, a “hard-looking Chicano with a missing tooth, a Fu Manchu mustache and a cobra tattoo on his right forearm” tells Simon what’s going on. “It’s a ‘wildcat,’” explains Snake, who seems happy to follow the crazy "white dudes” who started it all by “waving their arms, walking out, and shouting, ‘Join us!”. Other hard hats in the now idle crowd are pissed off about losing a few hours pay. “Anarchists,” one grumbles. “Commies and agitators. They don’t like it here, can’t blame them for that. But you can’t strike till the contract’s up. That’s the law.” A manager addresses the crowd with a bull-horn and repeats the same message. “This is an unlawful work stoppage. Your local union has not authorized this action, and joins us in ordering you to immediately cease and desist. This is your final warning.” A Tactical Error? The “cadre” organization members--who have inducted Simon into their small circle at a local radical bookstore--are among “the twelve people pegged as troublemakers and fired.” After this “tactical error,” Simon attends his first Steelworkers local union meeting. There, he encounters bureaucratic lethargy and business union routine familiar to many rank-and-file activists, then and now. Only a smattering of members show-up—at a VFW hall with an “American flag on the pole outside the building and another hung on a wall behind the podium.” Much time is spent on the financial report and a reading of minutes from the last meeting. The biggest agenda item is the e-board’s unanimous decision “not to pursue grievance arbitration cases for employees who were terminated.” As the union treasurer explains, this will result in “a big savings for the local because we could not have prevailed in defending an action that went against the ‘no strike’ clause in our own contract.” (“Good riddance,” blurts out the local’s business manager, “a pudgy man in a short sleeved white shirt,” who gavels the meeting to a close soon thereafter.) Bergman’s workplace descriptions are equally on target. Some resemble the best passages in The Jungle, Upton Sinclair’s fictional account of job hazards in mid-western meat-packing plants a century ago or in Emperor of Gladness , Ocean Voung’s new novel about low wage work in 21st century New England. “The smelter, known as ‘Freako,’ was a cavernous, ramshackle Big Top featuring spark-spewing furnaces, splashing cauldrons dangled from the cranes like murderous marionettes, rapids of liquid fire tumbling down in harrowing dayglow ribbons. Danger was everywhere, lurking beneath the dull roar and the rotten eggs stench. Everything black and orange, darkness and firelight, a waking nightmare Halloween that left him in terror of any possible misstep.” Unfortunately, the hottest shop floor issue is not the threat of being scalded to death or maimed and killed in many other ways. It’s ThreeCo’s controversial decision to hire its first female laborer, a feisty former high school athlete, who is a half-Latino and a single mother. It’s 1973, after all, and the era of equal opportunity is dawning. As the fictional reincarnation of Esperanza, Samantha Tanager is not just showing that she can, in a pinch, take a man’s place on the picket-line; she’s going to join them on the shop floor, in a fire-resistant orange jump suit, aluminum hard-hat, and steel-toed boots. But the sudden arrival of a “fetching copper miner’s daughter,” as a local newspaper describes her, proves to be very triggering for Bullock. He’s the big, tobacco-chewing redneck with “a natural talent for cruelty” that Bussbuam is assigned to work with. Already suspicious of Simon’s rather obvious East Coast Jewishness and college boy ways, Bullock views “Tanager’s admission to the sacred sanctum of the smelter as sacrilege, a grievous affront to the Code of the Working Stiff, Nonferrous Division.” Besides, he believes that Samantha is a lesbian. (Spoiler alert: much to Simon’s love-struck chagrin, Bullock’s gaydar is right.) Casual Racism Simon’s New Left idealism is now further tested amid Freako’s “dark, depraved beauty, which reeked of musty maleness that gave rise to a loose-knit, shambling ‘esprit de corps, wrapped in a kind of casual racism and sexism so expansive, so deeply rooted, it had started to feel—Simon not being of this world, and without standing perhaps to judge his co-workers’ cultural values—like just another flavor of assholism.” When that “assholism” takes the form of a nasty campaign by Bullock to make Tanager’s life miserable on the job, Simon’s own personal class struggle ends in a parking lot brawl between two “union brothers.” It doesn’t end well for the new hire and little resembles more heroic scuffles, between labor and management, in Salt of The Earth. But it does lead Bussbaum to bid blue-collar life adieu and head for the greener pastures of California. (Tanager and her female partner leave for the more tolerant Texas oasis of Austin.) Proles was definitely not written as a how-too manual for members of the Rank-and-File Project , a present-day effort to “recruit, educate, and support a new generation of activists who will join the fight for working-class power by taking union jobs on the shop floor.” But the book should be required reading, in such circles anyway, due to its deft exploration of the nexus between the personal and the political. Any left-wing “salt” trying to befriend un-class conscious (and sometimes weird) co-workers, while dealing with draining night shifts, imperious managers and not much nicer union bosses, will find humorous respite in Barry Bergman’s fictional rendering of his real-life experience with the “salt of the earth” in Arizona fifty years ago.

articles.title: Press Release: MN Chapters of the DSA Condemn Escalating Zenophobic Attacks Against Our Somali and Immigrant Communities
articles.author: Twin Ports DSA
articles.content: We, the undersigned DSA chapters of the State of Minnesota, denounce and strongly condemn the escalation of xenophobic rhetoric that the Trump administration is intentionally directing at our communities. The President’s recent othering and dehumanizing of Minnesota's Somali communities encourages violence, both from his supporters and the violent and unaccountable national security state. Minnesota is stronger because of our Somali and other immigrant communities. Immigrants are our friends, co-workers, teachers, community leaders, and more. As Minnesotans, we know who we are and we won’t fall for dishonest actors spreading disinformation and hateful, divisive rhetoric about our immigrant neighbors. No Minnesotan should feel unsafe or unwelcome because of their faith, heritage, or background. We stand in solidarity with our Somali and immigrant neighbors, and the Minnesota 15 who are facing retaliatory punishment for standing alongside our community. This past winter, armed agents of the fascist federal government attempted to tear down our communities by force. But Minnesotans’ depth of organized resistance cannot be dismantled. We have organized by the thousands across race, class, and faith to effectively defend our neighbors and communities. We built a decentralized network based on the collective awareness and shared vision that we all deserve to live, thrive, and be protected in our places of work, worship, and homes. We have shown the world that the vast majority of Americans will not tolerate our communities being turned into high tech laboratories of surveillance and occupation. We have shown the world that we will not accept having our hardworking neighbors terrorized and disappeared out of their homes. In response to our show of street power, fascist politicians are once again using lies about immigrants in an attempt to incite fear, violence, and division. They think this tactic will help them win the upcoming midterm elections, but we are united in our vision for justice, liberation, and a better world. They fear our movements because we are powerful, principled, and we are angry. As the Minnesota chapters of the Democratic Socialists of America, we encourage our members and our neighbors to keep showing up for one another. Join your neighborhood group, host a community dinner, check in with a friend, get plugged into rapid response, and of course, join DSA and organize your community! Stay strong. Solidarity and sincerity forever. SIGNED: Twin Ports DSA, Twin Cities DSA, Brainerd Lakes Area DSA, St. Cloud DSA, Red River Valley DSA, Southeast Minnesota DSA

articles.title: The Margin of Effort: How Election Volunteering Can Help Save Democracy
articles.author: Paul Rogat Loeb
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Sometimes it’s the humble actions that matter, an important lesson for our dangerous time. For years, I’ve volunteered to get out the vote for my preferred candidates. In one election, knocking on doors in a Seattle neighborhood, I spoke with three people who supported my candidate for governor but wouldn’t have voted had I not contacted them: One forgot it was Election Day. Another didn’t know how to submit an absentee ballot. The third needed a ride to the polls. My impact had nothing to do with eloquence or skill and everything to do with simply showing up. After three recounts, my candidate won by 133 votes in a state of 6.2 million. I’d personally gotten one-fiftieth of the margin. If just a handful of the volunteers on my side had stayed home, or there had been a few more on the other side, Washington State would have had a different governor. Related: Poll Workers, Essential for Our Democracy Another time, in a US Senate race, I walked Election Day precincts until my feet hurt, and then continued until the polls closed. The margin this time was 2,229 votes, and I had no idea it would be that close. I also once invited my neighbors to a house party for my friend Lisa, who was running for Seattle City Council. Fifteen people RSVP’d, but only five showed, plus Lisa and her campaign manager. I apologized for wasting the campaign’s time, but my friend Shep, who’d just retired, was one of the five. He bombarded her with questions, but then, profoundly impressed by her answers, made volunteering for her campaign his full-time job over the next five weeks. Lisa won by 39 votes. Had we not held the house party, she most likely would have lost. Many of us spend hours a day inhaling the bad news of our dark reality. Or we follow the polls like we do our favorite sports teams, elated when our candidates rise, deflated when they fall. Knowing what’s going on is important, but if we put at least some of that energy into electing candidates we believe in, we can change the results, including America’s critical upcoming midterms. The research confirms our potential impact. A 2024 analysis by political scientists Christopher B. Mann and Katherine Haenschen found that in high-visibility elections like midterms, each potential voter you talk with adds 3 percentage points to the likelihood that they’ll vote. So if you reach 100 people from a list predisposed toward your candidate, you’ll likely generate three additional votes from people who’d probably otherwise stay home. Volunteer phone calls produce a shade less, 2.3 points per person reached. Neither sounds like much, but if 10,000 volunteers each spend two days and reach 100 voters, that will yield roughly 30,000 votes. That’s larger than the margin for a half dozen of the 2022 Senate and governor races, during which only 31% of eligible young voters showed up . If you still feel too bleak to volunteer, or the candidates don’t meet your perfect standard, remember that people have far more room to act before would-be dictators consolidate power. Recently, I met a young Russian woman who joined the protests around Putin’s jailing of dissident Alexei Navalny. “But then they got smaller and the risks got greater,” she said. So she stopped. As Navalny, who died in a Siberian prison, wrote in his memoir, “While we were immersed in our petty squabbles to decide whom to label as belonging to which faction, and whether it was appropriate for us to be photographed in their company, we suddenly found ourselves living in a country where people were being thrown in prison for no reason or even murdered.” Courageous and impactful action is possible even under dictatorships, as when Argentina’s Mothers of the Disappeared demanded the military tell them the fate of their children and helped bring down that murderous regime. But it’s far easier when dictatorial power is still contested and doesn’t control every major institution. So if we want to preserve our democracy, this election is a maximum point of leverage to act. And that means doing all we can now to impact it by knocking on doors, making phone calls, sending letters and postcards, texting our friends and asking others to do the same, supporting grassroots efforts in key states and districts. Pollsters talk about “the margin of error,” which means their projections aren’t cast in stone. Organizers talk about the “margin of effort,” which is what happens when enough ordinary people join a campaign and reach out to others. The more each of us can become part of that margin, the better our chances. Adapted from Paul Loeb’s The Impossible Will Take a Little While: Perseverance and Hope in Troubled Times theimpossible.org or order here . This appeared first in The Fulcrum.

articles.title: Britain’s Military-Industrial Complex Is Promoting War Fever
articles.author: John Rees
articles.content: War fever has gripped the European political establishment. War in Ukraine and rumors of continent-wide conflict with Russia are now the staple justification for rearmament, ballooning arms budgets, and the reintroduction of conscription across Europe. Popular consent for this lurch to militarization is very limited indeed, so the political establishment is deploying military and security service officers, past and present, in an unprecedented propaganda blitz to make the case for war. Astounding statistics underline how far this process has gone. In the last twelve months, there have been approximately nine hundred appearances by serving or former military or security service officers on Britain’s mainstream media. That’s roughly seventy-five contributions every month, or seventeen a week. The figure would be much higher if pro-war politicians were included. In other words, the military and the secret services have been broadcasting on, or writing in, British media outlets more than twice a day, every day, for a full year. Khaki Media Let’s look at some specific cases. Former Air Vice-Marshal Sean Bell alone has appeared multiple times, partly as a result of being employed as Sky News’ military analyst. His defense consultancy, rarely acknowledged, provides strategic defense advice to national and international clients, leveraging his senior Royal Air Force (RAF) experience — which included overseeing military contracts and projects with Saudi Arabia. Sir Patrick Sanders, former chief of the General Staff, has appeared repeatedly in the last year, including on Channel 4 News and in The Times . He’s a defense adviser to Santander Bank and chair of strategic intelligence at Herminius. Last year, the government Advisory Committee on Business Appointments had to issue a warning letter imposing restrictions on Sanders’s work. This was because it found that, in view of his military background, there was a “significant risk that he could offer Herminius unfair access and influence” should it or its clients “wish to influence policy decisions and/or work with government.” Major General Rupert Jones, former Standing Joint Force commander, is a media regular, including serial appearances on Sky News. He is an adviser to Skyral, which builds artificial intelligence technology for the defense, national security, and enterprise sectors. The firm has contracts with the UK and US governments and with NATO. The major general has further commitments as a partner and head of strategy execution at Strategia Worldwide, which conducts business risk assessment, and a consultant at Berwicks Consultants, which manages risk and crisis response. He also works for Pallas Advisors, which advises tech companies on national security — not to mention the fact that three years ago, he became a senior adviser at IBM. The former commander of the Joint Forces Command, Sir Richard Barrons, has frequently made media appearances in the last twelve months. This year, he has been arguing publicly for substantially higher UK defense expenditure, with an extra £10 billion a year. He is also founder and cochairman of Universal Defence and Security Solutions (UDSS), a defense and security consultancy. This affiliation was not disclosed alongside his commentary. While Bell, Jones, Sanders, and Barrons are the most frequent TV and press military advocates of arms production, they are far from alone. Lord David Richards, Sir Mark Carleton-Smith, Sir Peter Wall, and Sir Nick Carter, all of whom are former chiefs of the Defence Staff or the General Staff, have made multiple appearances. They have been joined in this propaganda effort by figures like Sir Richard Shirreff, a former senior NATO officer; Sir Chris Deverell, former commander of the Joint Forces Command; and a host of others. Spooks on Air We can find a legion of senior secret service bosses right alongside these military figures. Until recently, it would have been unheard of for the public even to know the names of serving or retired security chiefs. It was only in 2010 that Sir John Sawers became the first “C” — the head of MI6 — to deliver a public speech . Now leading spooks are all over the airwaves bolstering the new militarism. The UK intelligence chiefs use a strategy described as “more open to stay secret.” Instead of staying completely in the shadows, modern spy chiefs treat public relations as a strategic tool to propagandize for government policy, recruit, and maintain public trust. The current head of MI6 and three former heads of MI6, the current director general of MI5, the former CEO of the National Cyber Security Centre, and the former director of Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) have all made public interventions and appeared on media outlets that include the BBC, Sky News, and The Guardian . The director general of MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, delivers televised annual addresses from MI5 headquarters. In September 2026, he took to the pages of the Independent to publish a high-profile “call to arms,” warning the public of state-sponsored threats from Russia and China. In December 2025, the newly appointed chief of MI6, Blaise Metreweli, used her inaugural public speech to explicitly warn that the UK is operating in “a space between peace and war,” directly identifying cyber threats and information warfare from Russia and China. In 2022, the spy-media love-in went so far that the BBC invited GCHQ Director Jeremy Fleming to guest edit Radio 4’s flagship news program Today . The media blitz by the security services is so extensive that even some people deep in the political establishment are worried it may all be too much. The UK’s intelligence watchdog, the Intelligence and Security Committee of Parliament, has said the media work by senior spies has gotten out of hand. Such media appearances were becoming so frequent that “they risk trivialising the important work of the Agencies” and could end up “diverting their focus from national security priorities.” It also seems to have worried about the spymasters getting sucked into spats on social media with bots, since “social media is also known to be a battleground for covert hostile state action.” This warning came from a committee whose members include Lord Alan West, himself a frequent military media pundit. Parade Ground Academics The generals and the spooks have a (much smaller) supporting chorus of academics. Some academics appearing in the media are critical of the new drive to war, like Paul Rogers of Bradford University’s School of Peace Studies. But they are a small minority. Most academic commentators do not come from universities but from establishment think tanks with close links to the military and security apparatus, like Chatham House and the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI). Matthew Savill, director of military sciences at the RUSI, spent over twenty years at the Ministry of Defence. He began his career in 2003 as an Iraq analyst and was seconded to the Cabinet Office National Security Secretariat. Emily Ferris, senior associate fellow at RUSI, is a senior Russia analyst for Control Risks, a major corporate intelligence and security firm. Nicholas Hopton, chairman of the Advisory Board for the Middle East strand and Mediterranean program at the Centre for Geopolitics at the University of Cambridge, served as the British ambassador in a series of Middle Eastern and North African countries — Yemen, Qatar, Libya, and Iran — between 2012 and 2021. Crucially, he worked in the UK Cabinet Office, where he drafted the UK’s first-ever National Security Strategy in 2008. Dr H. A. Hellyer, senior associate fellow in international security studies at RUSI, was appointed deputy convenor of the UK government’s Task Force on Tackling Radicalisation and Extremism after the 2005 London bombings. The contrast with the much more limited mainstream media presence of antiwar voices is stark. The combined media footprint of the military and security spokespeople, plus the think tankers, accounts for roughly 90 percent of all appearances about war and security issues. Representatives of antiwar organizations have to make do with the remaining 10 percent. Even when antiwar activists get a hearing, the interviews are often not about government policy, military threats, or the politics of ongoing conflicts but about the nature, or policing, of the protests they help organize. If the comparison is restricted to occasions where contributors are invited specifically to interpret war, defense, or foreign policy, as opposed to being interviewed about a protest, the disparity is even starker — something in the region of thirty to one. Hard Power The state’s mission creep into the media is not the only way that increasingly politicized arms of the state are shaping events. Sir Mark Rowley, perhaps the most overtly ideological commissioner London’s Metropolitan Police has ever had, is playing the role of a politician as much as that of a policeman, without having gone through the tedious bother of being elected. Recently, he effectively overrode London Mayor Sadiq Khan by pushing to get Palantir reinstated in a tech trial for the Met Police, despite the mayor’s very real fears about the notorious corporation. Rowley is spearheading the Met’s crackdown on Palestine protesters, arresting more than two thousand people for acts of solidarity with Palestinians, many of whom have been detained under terrorism legislation that was never supposed to be used against civil political protest. Rowley himself is a very politically engaged figure, especially in his dealings with supporters of Israel. He has held private meetings with Israeli Ambassador Tzipi Hotovely, and he has spoken at the annual conference of an Israeli think tank linked to the country’s military and intelligence services. In March this year, Rowley attended a dinner hosted by the Community Security Trust (CST), a group that equates anti-Zionism with antisemitism and aggressively targets critics of Israel. On his watch, the Met has invited the CST into its special operations room during the monitoring of pro-Palestine protests. The Starmer government’s ban on Palestine Action under terrorism legislation has triggered a 660 percent increase in arrests for “terrorism,” mostly involving people who were nabbed for holding a sign expressing support for the proscribed group. If these arrestees are actually convicted — and many are being tried in no-jury courts — there will be more political prisoners in the UK than in Vladimir Putin’s Russia. The Military-Industrial Complex US President Dwight Eisenhower coined the term “military-industrial complex” in his 1961 farewell address. Who can deny the contemporary relevance of Eisenhower’s description of this “immense military establishment,” whose influence was “felt in every city, every state house, every office of the federal government” and that affected “the very structure of our society”? Eisenhower’s warning that “the potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist,” and that such power could “endanger our liberties or democratic processes,” also feels strikingly topical. Eisenhower certainly did not want an end to US military power — he simply wanted it to be more carefully managed. But the term has outlived him, and it remains useful in describing how militarism and capitalism work in the imperial core of the system. There is some danger that the term can be misused if it diminishes our ability to see how other very powerful capitalist interests, such as Big Oil or Big Pharma, wield power in the state. But there are phases of imperial development where the military-industrial complex becomes the dominant driver of events. The current massive rearmament drive in Europe looks very much like such a moment. Advocates of austerity, who previously justified it in terms of the supposed need to “balance the books” on the good-housekeeping model, now tend to present it as a way to free up resources so we can rearm for a European war that is only years away. European leaders copy Donald Trump’s rearmament binge, not least because they fear that Washington’s “pivot to the Pacific” is leaving them militarily exposed to a greater degree than at any time since World War II. The propaganda war is a major part of this development. It is necessary precisely because the whole war preparation project is hitting a wall of public skepticism. In one poll , 50 percent of young people aged sixteen to twenty-nine in the UK said they would never fight for Britain under any circumstances. An additional 38 percent would do so only “under some circumstances.” This is part of a wider disillusionment with the way society is structured. Only 36 percent believe their lives will be better than those of their parents (down from 63 percent the previous year), while 38 percent believe their lives will be worse. Just 25 percent feel the political system treats them fairly, and 56 percent agree that democracy in Britain is in trouble. Popular consciousness is always formed by three contradictory factors: what the establishment tells people is true, what their own experience tells them is true, and what the experience of struggle teaches them is true. In Britain and its European neighbors, the establishment is telling people things about war that conflict with their own experience of its effects in the period since the invasion of Iraq. From the anti-conscription demonstrations in Germany involving hundreds of thousands of high school students to the blockades by students in France, the mass protests over housing in Spain, and the international Palestine solidarity movement, there are plenty of signs that the ruling bombocracy will not find it easy to march us all down the road to war.
